In the basmala and the opening of the surah: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful."

﴿Ta-Sin-Mim﴾ (1):

﴿Ta-Sin-Mim﴾ (1) (al-Shu'ara'):

We have already spoken about the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) at the beginnings of the surahs, and we said: there is a difference between the name of a letter (ism al-harf) and the sound it denotes (musamma al-harf). The sound of the letter ba', for example, is "ba" or "bu" or "bi" or "ib" when it is unvowelled; its name, however, is "ba'" with a fatha, or with a damma, or with a sukun. But when you pronounce this letter in a word such as kataba, you pronounce the sound of the letter, not its name.

And we said: this matter has many meanings, the simplest of which is that the Qur'an, which is the miraculous speech of Allah, is sent down from letters like your letters with which you speak, and words like those in your language. But what is it that made it distinct in its miraculousness from your speech? We say: because it is the speech of Allah. This is the difference; as for the letters, they are one and the same.

And if you reflect, you will find that the disjointed letters at the beginnings of the surahs total fourteen letters(1), which are half of the letters of the alphabet. Sometimes one letter comes, sometimes two, sometimes three, sometimes four, and sometimes five. This shows us that the Qur'an is miraculous even though it is made of the same letters as yours and the same words as yours.

We have already given an example to clarify this matter: suppose you wished to test a group of people in skilled weaving, so you gave one of them wool, to a second silk, to a third cotton, and to a fourth linen. Could you judge the fineness of each one's weaving, and which is finer and more beautiful? Of course not, because silk is softer and finer than cotton, cotton is finer than wool, and wool is finer than linen. If you want to distinguish precision and skill in this craft, you must unify the material type.

So, the miracle of the Qur'an is that its material and the material of other speech are one: letters and words. Therefore, the Blessed and Exalted Truth often says, after the disjointed letters: ﴿That are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ (2).

1 These fourteen letters are gathered in our saying: "Nass hakim qati' lahu sirr" (a wise, decisive text that has a secret). Al-Zamakhshari said: these fourteen letters comprise the categories of letter types, namely: of the whispered and the voiced, of the soft and the hard, of the emphatic and the open, of the elevated and the lowered, and of the echoing letters (huruf al-qalqalah). Glory be to Him in whose every thing His wisdom is precise. (Cited by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir, 1/37).

Meaning: that the Clear Book is composed of letters such as these, and God, exalted be He, has other meanings in it, containing intentions of His, which time may perhaps reveal to us.... The Qur'an is the speech of God, and His attributes are infinite in perfection. If you are able to describe things—this is such-and-such, and that is such-and-such—then this is the capacity of man and of the human intellect. As for the verses of God in His Clear Book, they are the distinct verses which have a beginning and an end, and the surahs of the Qur'an are composed of them.

Then the Almighty says:

﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not believe.﴾ (26:3)

This is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because he burdened himself in conveying the message beyond what he could bear, and beyond what Allah required of him, out of his eagerness for the guidance of people and for their return to the way of Allah, so that they might deserve to be successors on the earth. Also, among the conditions of faith is that you love for your brother what you love for yourself.(1)

And the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, consoles His Messenger (ﷺ), as He said to him in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their footsteps if they do not believe in this message.﴾ (18:6)

It is as when you see your son exhausting himself in study, and you pity him lest he destroy himself; you reproach him for his own benefit. Likewise, the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, reproaches His Messenger out of compassion and fear for him, lest he destroy himself.

The meaning of ﴿bākhiʿ﴾ (باخع, "killing yourself") in (26:3): al-bakhʿ (البخع) is slaughter that does not stop at cutting the windpipe and the two jugular veins(2), but goes to the extreme until it severs the vertebrae and draws out the spinal cord from between them. The meaning is: you grieve a deep grief that takes hold of you until you perish. This indicates the hardship that the Messenger (ﷺ) was suffering from his people's denial of him.

In another place, He says to His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿So do not let yourself be consumed in regret over them.﴾ (35:8) This is a clear and definitive command and an explicit prohibition, after He drew his attention with disapproval, saying: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself...﴾ (26:3).

Allah, exalted is He, has alerted His Messenger in several places so that he would not burden himself beyond his capacity. He, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿Your duty is only to convey, and upon Us is the account.﴾ (13:40)

And He said: ﴿You are not over them a controller.﴾ (88:22)

And He said: ﴿And you are not over them a compeller.﴾ (50:45)

So the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, says to His Messenger: Be gentle with yourself, and do not impose on it a severe, exhausting burden. This reproach is for the benefit of the Messenger, not against him.

(1) On the authority of Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand my soul is, no servant believes until he loves for his neighbor—or he said: for his brother—what he loves for himself." A hadith agreed upon. Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (13), and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (45), Book of Faith.

(2) Al-wadajan (الودجان): two veins connected from the head to the base of the throat. The plural is awdaj, which are the veins surrounding the windpipe; when the awdaj are cut, it is called wadaja. (Lisan al-Arab, root w-d-j)

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them from the sky a sign, before which their necks would remain humbly subdued.﴾

The sign here is not a sign that persuades minds; rather, it is a sign that compels them and subdues their necks, subduing their physique and form. This is not a theoretical statement addressed to the deniers; rather, these are realities that actually occurred among the Children of Israel. Read, if you wish, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We raised the mountain above them as though it were a canopy, and they thought it would fall upon them: "Take hold of what We have given you with strength...﴾ (al-A'raf: 171).

So they took what We had given them with strength. Why? Because of the sign that compelled them and subdued their forms. But the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, as we have said, does not desire that faith subdue forms; rather, He desires that it subdue hearts through certainty and following.

Had your Lord willed, He would have made everyone on earth believe, all of them, without any of them differing. The proof is that He, glorified is He, created the angels who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and do what they are commanded. And the proof is that He, glorified is He, sent messengers and protected them, and did not give Satan any way over them. And the proof is that Satan, after he pledged to lead the children of Adam astray so that they would be equal with him in disobedience, was told by Him: ﴿Indeed, over My servants you shall have no authority...﴾ (al-Hijr: 42).

And Satan himself says: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, except among them Your chosen servants who are sincere.﴾ (Sad: 82–83).

Therefore: had He willed, He would have made all people believers, and that would not have been difficult for Him. But He, glorified is He, willed that faith be by the choice of the believer, coming willingly and by choice.

Even in worldly affairs and among their people, you may see a tyrant striking people and subduing them to his command and prohibition, so they obey him with the obedience of forms. But can he, by his tyranny, subdue their hearts?

And He said: ﴿So their necks would remain humbly subdued to it.﴾ (al-Shu'ara': 4). He singled out the necks because they are the manifestation of submission; the first of submission is that necks bend. Or "necks" in the Arabic usage refers to the faces and notables of a people; therefore they say in warning: "This is a matter in which necks will be lost."

What is meant is: the great necks, those of high standing, not the necks of the common people, the weak, or the powerless. Similarly the expression "the chests of the people" means their notables and leading figures who fill the eyes.

The meaning is: you do not subdue people, for if I wanted to subdue them I would have subdued them. Therefore the Exalted says in another verse: ﴿And had your Lord willed, all those on earth would have believed together. Would you then compel people until they become believers?﴾ (Yunus: 99).

If your Lord does not compel people to faith, will you compel them? And why compulsion in the religion of Allah? The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, continues to send down the Qur'an to them, verse after verse, so that perhaps a star from its stars might coincide with an empty space and a heart clear of resentment toward the Messenger of Allah, and so it believes.

But far-fetched is it for such people, who have been stamped with obstinacy, contentiousness and denial, to believe. Therefore Allah says of them: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance...﴾ (al-Naml: 14).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 26, verse 5:

He said about them:

﴿And there does not come to them any new reminder from the Most Merciful, but they turn away from it.﴾

His saying ﴿new [muhdath]...﴾ means: new to their minds, because We do not confront them with one verse alone, but with verses one after another. ﴿But they turn away from it.﴾

So whenever a verse came to them, they denied it. This is evidence of the obstinacy (ladd) and the enmity that never leave their hearts toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), such that no star of the Qur'an encounters empty hearts. It is as if their enmity toward you, O Muhammad, has prevented them from believing in the Qur'an; they would be ready to believe in the Qur'an if it came from someone other than you.

Did they not say: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?﴾

Therefore, obstinacy and contention are not in the method of Allah, but in the person of the Messenger of Allah. For this reason your Lord consoles you and cares for you: ﴿We know that what they say grieves you...﴾ once a sorcerer, once a madman... etc.

Look at the consolation: ﴿So it is not you they deny...﴾ To them you are truthful and trustworthy, ﴿but it is the wrongdoers who reject the signs of Allah.﴾

His exalted saying ﴿but they turn away from it﴾ means: in dullness and obstinacy. And is there anyone more obstinate than their saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾

instead of saying: "Guide us to it!"

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 26, verse 6:

﴿So they have denied, but there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾

That is: whenever a reminder from the Most Merciful came to them, and a sign from His signs, they persisted in denying it. ﴿So there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾ (al-Shu'ara')

As comes in other verses: ﴿And those who have wronged will know by what return they will be returned.﴾ (al-Shu'ara', 227)

And He said: ﴿And you will surely know its news after a while.﴾ (Sad, 88)

That is: tomorrow you will know the outcome of your denial. The signs of God are moving ahead of you. Every day the believers in Muhammad increase and the number of disbelievers decreases; every day the land of faith expands and the land of unbelief recedes.

Did not the Truthful, glorified and exalted, say to them: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its edges...?﴾ (al-Anbiya', 44)

So these are, then, preliminary signs that you see with your own eyes, and it was incumbent upon you to take from them a lesson and an admonition. The early signs of the success of the call and the manifestation of the religion are clear. This is the meaning of: ﴿So there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾ (al-Shu'ara')

Would that they had confined themselves to denial and persistence in it. Rather, the matter among them went beyond that to mockery of the messengers and of the words of God. Did they not say, by way of mockery: ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ (al-Furqan, 41)

¹ al-Munqalab (المنقلب): a noun of place/time meaning the act of turning over; returning to God means going back to Him and being transformed. Al-Munqalab: the destination of servants in the Hereafter. (Lisan al-Arab, root q-l-b)

Then the Exalted says:

﴿Have they not seen the earth, how many noble pairs of every kind We have caused to grow therein?﴾ (26:7)

When the repeated reminder and the renewed signs failed to move these obstinate people, and they did not turn back, God, the Exalted, referred them to the cosmic signs that are manifest to them and that existed before them in being: signs in the heavens, the sun, the moon and the stars; and signs on the earth, the seas, the deserts, the mountains, the plants and the animals.

All of these are cosmic signs that none of them created. Rather, man came into existence and arrived upon them, and these signs that they see preceded him: the great and the small, the man and the woman, the rational and the non-rational. Do they not look at them with a glance of consideration, so that they might ask about their Originator?

We set for this an example: a man who has been cut off from the ways in a barren desert, until he is near to perishing; then sleep overtakes him and he sleeps. When he awakes, he finds in this isolated place a table upon which are the finest foods and drinks. Should he not, before his hand reaches out to this food, ask himself: who prepared it for him?

Likewise, man has come upon a universe prepared to receive him, and upon an existence that his power does not encompass, and over which he has no authority. He does not, for instance, bring the sun into being so as to kindle it, and no one among them created these cosmic signs. Does this not point to the Creator (Mighty and Majestic) and make belief in Him obligatory upon us?

For this reason He, glorified be He, says: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "God..."﴾ (31:25).

And He said: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created them?" they would surely say, "God..."﴾ (43:87).

Consider the small bulb that lights a room, whose expected lifespan does not exceed a few months, and which is liable to break and to malfunction. Yet a team of engineers, workers and technicians, and many machines and tools, have combined in its manufacture. Nevertheless, we date the inventor of the lamp, we know its history and how it was made, and so on. We know the inventor of the telephone and the radio, and so on.

Is it not more fitting that we look and reflect upon the creation of the sun, this great celestial body that lights the whole world, without fuel, spare parts, or malfunction throughout these successive ages?

Then, if a messenger comes and breaks this heedlessness for the people, and says to them: "Shall I inform you of who created all this? It is God." It would be incumbent upon them to lend him their ears and believe.

Here He, exalted be He, says: ﴿Have they not seen the earth...﴾ (26:7). It is a manifest sign before their eyes: they see it lifeless, barren and desolate; then, when water descends upon it, God revives it with vegetation. Have they not looked at the mountains and the desert after the rain has fallen, and how they clothe themselves in a wondrous garment of plants after the winter season?

Did they not ask themselves: who transported these seeds and sowed them in the mountains? For this reason He, glorified be He, says elsewhere: ﴿And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and grows every delightful pair.﴾ (22:5).

His saying here: ﴿how many noble pairs of every kind We have caused to grow therein﴾ (26:7). "Kam" (كم) is an informative particle indicating abundance, and it came in the form of an interrogative for affirmation, as you say to your companion, "How much have I done good to you?" instead of enumerating the manifestations of your kindness toward him. You ask because you are confident the answer is in your favour; so the statement is by way of information, a call from you, but the answer to a question is an acknowledgment from him. The meaning, then, is that the plant-life of the earth is abundant beyond counting.

"Zawj" (زوج) means a kind, and also a male or a female. Some of the common people think that "zawj" means two, and this is an error: "zawj" is one together with its like, as in His saying: ﴿eight pairs: of the sheep two, and of the goats two. Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain? Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful." And of the camels two, and of the cattle two...﴾ (6:143–144).

These are four kinds containing eight individuals, so "zawj" is a single unit together with its like. You do not say "a zawj of shoes" but "two shoes." The Almighty says: ﴿And that He created the pairs, the male and the female﴾ (53:45).

Likewise, plants must have a male and a female aspect, even if it is not clear in all of them as it is clear, for example, in the palm tree, where there is a male from which we fertilise the female so that she bears fruit; and similarly the jumair tree has a male and a female. But we have not seen male and female in the guava or the lemon tree, for example. Why?

They said: sometimes male and female exist in one thing, such as the maize stalk: before it produces its fruit, a tassel emerges at its top bearing the male pollen, and when the wind shakes it, the pollen falls onto the cob (kuz) of the maize and pollination is completed. And sometimes the male and female are in something you do not know, such as the mango and the apple, so we have not known for them a male and a female.

But the Exalted says: ﴿And We sent the winds fertilising...﴾ (15:22).

And He said: ﴿And of everything We created pairs...﴾ (51:49).

Then He described the pair as ﴿noble﴾ (26:7). What does nobility mean here? They said: because if you take a single fruit and look at it and reflect upon it, you will find in it many attributes and numerous blessings, as He, glorified be He, says: ﴿And if you count God's blessings, you will not number them...﴾ (14:34), where it is "blessing" in the singular form, and He did not say "the blessings of God."

They said: because the Exalted wishes to draw our attention to the fact that every single blessing, if its components and makeup were examined, would reveal within it blessings beyond number and count.

So the meaning of ﴿noble﴾ (26:7) is: abundant in bounty and abundant in goodness.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 8:

﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them are not believers.﴾

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign...﴾ (al-Shu'ara'), meaning: in the sign of growth, and every noble pair that comes forth from the earth, ﴿is a sign...﴾ (al-Shu'ara'), a wondrous thing and a clear indication of a wise Creator who acts with purpose and order. It should draw our attention to the power of the Creator, Mighty and Majestic is He.

﴿But most of them are not believers﴾ (al-Shu'ara'), meaning: despite all these signs, they did not believe, except a few of them, as the Exalted said in another verse: ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth do they pass by, while they turn away from it?﴾ (Yusuf, 105). Yet if you reflect on a single sign, it would be sufficient to turn your attention to God. In everything there is a sign indicating that He is One.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And indeed your Lord — He is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾

Here the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, mentions the attribute "the Mighty" (al-'Aziz) after saying ﴿And most of them were not believers﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 8), so that we know that those who disbelieved did not disbelieve against Allah's will; rather, they disbelieved by means of the choice (ikhtiyar) that Allah deposited in them.

So He, glory be to Him, is the One who aided them in it, since they loved it and persisted in it; for He, exalted is He, is their Lord. The proof is that if He had left them compelled and forced, they would never have done anything contrary to the way of Allah. And the proof is that they are now compelled in matters and subdued in their lives in many affairs, and yet none of them can rebel against any of that.

Despite their habitual obstinacy and rebellion against the way of Allah, can any one of them resist sickness, or death, or the decrees that descend upon him? Does any of them choose the day of his birth, for example, or the day of his death? Does he choose his height, his strength, or his intelligence?

But when Allah gave them capability and choice, they chose disbelief, so Allah aided them in what they loved, and He sealed their hearts so that disbelief would not leave them and faith would not enter them.

The word "al-'Aziz" means: the One who is not overcome and not subdued. But this attribute is not sufficient with regard to Him, exalted is He, because it implies equality with the opposite; so we must add to it that He, glory be to Him, is also the Dominant.

Therefore He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And Allah is dominant over His affair﴾ (Yusuf 21). So Allah, exalted is He, is Mighty: He overcomes and is not overcome.

An example of that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He feeds but is not fed﴾ (al-An'am 14).

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Who has in His hand the dominion of all things, and He protects [them] while none can protect against Him?"﴾ (al-Mu'minun 88).

Then He, glory be to Him, mentions after it the attribute of mercy. He, glory be to Him, is Merciful together with His might. He, exalted is He, is merciful even when He prevails. Did He not follow up for them the signs and leave them to reflection and contemplation, perhaps they would return to their right senses and believe? When they persisted in disbelief, He gave them respite and did not seize them with the punishment of total annihilation, as He seized the other nations when they denied their messengers.

The messengers before Muhammad (ﷺ) used to convey the call and display the miracle, and whoever did not believe after that, Allah would punish him, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿So each We seized for his sin. Among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of stones, and among them were those seized by the blast, and among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them were those whom We drowned﴾ (al-'Ankabut 40).

As for the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), the Exalted has said concerning it: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾ (al-Anfal 33).

And here He said: ﴿And indeed your Lord — He is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 9). So the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, in all these verses consoles His Messenger (ﷺ) and gives him a lesson from the messengers who preceded him. Muhammad is not a novelty (bid'a) in this matter. Did not his Lord say to him: ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them except that they used to mock him﴾ (Ya-Sin 30)? So the matter, then, is ancient — as ancient as the messages.

(1) bida': (badi' or 'ajib — strange or wondrous). It is said: "So-and-so is a bida' in the matter," meaning he was the first to do it. Allah says: ﴿Say: "I am not a novelty among the messengers..."﴾ (al-Ahqaf 9), meaning: I am not strange, nor wondrous, nor was I without a precedent; rather I am like the messengers before me. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/57).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 10:

Therefore the context then takes us to the procession of the prophets, and the Truth, glory be to Him, mentions to His Messenger (ﷺ) a portion of the story of the Prophet Musa (Moses):

﴿And when your Lord called out to Musa: "Go to the wrongdoing people"﴾ (26:10).

Allah, blessed and exalted, relates to His Messenger the stories of the prophets, and they are the best of stories, for wisdom: ﴿And We relate to you the news of the messengers, by which We strengthen your heart...﴾ (Hud 11:120).

For the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went through many battles with disbelief, so he needed continuous strengthening whenever he faced hardship. Therefore the Qur'anic narratives are repeated for the Messenger throughout the length of the da'wah (call to Islam). The Qur'anic story is not intended as a history of the lives of the earlier messengers; rather it is to give the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) a lesson and an admonition from those of his brother messengers who came before him. Therefore the story comes in several places, and in each place there is a particular snapshot that suits the event in which it was revealed.

Here He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And when your Lord called out to Musa...﴾ (26:10), meaning: Remember, O Muhammad, when your Lord called out to Musa, that is, summoned him.

But why did He begin with the story of Musa, peace be upon him, in particular?

They said: Because the disbelievers of Makkah disbelieved in you, so do not grieve; for others were more heinous than them, as one who claimed divinity and said: ﴿I do not know of any god for you other than me...﴾ (28:38).

The context here does not mention where his Lord called to him, nor when He called to him, and the dialogue with him begins directly; but in other places the details of all this come.

Then comes the direct command from Allah the Exalted to His Prophet Musa: ﴿That you go to the wrongdoing people﴾ (26:10), that is, those who wronged themselves by making a partner for Allah, the Exalted, and shirk is the pinnacle of wrongdoing: ﴿Indeed, shirk is a great wrong﴾ (Luqman 31:13).

The Qur'an does not specify who these wrongdoers are, because they are well known and famous; in the realm of shirk they need no introduction, so that when we say "the wrongdoing people" (26:10), the mind turns to them: to Pharaoh and his people, for he was the only one who dared to claim divinity.

Then, after describing them, He identifies them: ﴿The people of Pharaoh. Will they not be mindful of God?﴾

That is: say to them, O Moses, "Will you not fear your Lord?" and present this proposition to them, because a request may come as a plain command, "Do such-and-such," or it may come gently, in the form of a proposal: "Will you not do such-and-such?" by way of interrogation, presentation and urging (ḥaḍḍ).

The meaning is: will they not fear God in their wronging of themselves by taking a partner with God, when there is no god but Him? And they wronged the Children of Israel in that they slaughtered their sons and spared their women.

But why does He speak of the people of Pharaoh first, and not address Pharaoh himself first, when he is the head of corruption among the people?

The answer to this question is the well-known saying: "O Pharaoh, what made you a tyrant?" He said: "Because I found no one to stop me." Had his people stood up to him and restrained him, he would have desisted. But they left him alone; rather, they followed in his wake until he became a tyrant, and they helped him until he became an idol of oppression (ṭāghūt).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 12:

Then Musa said:

﴿My Lord, I fear that they will deny me.﴾

When Allah, blessed and exalted is He, called His Prophet Musa, peace be upon him, to go to the people of Pharaoh, he did not rush to go. Rather, he expressed to his Lord the misgivings and disquiet of his soul, because he knew in advance the hardship of this mission. He had lived with Pharaoh and knew his nature. So he said: ﴿I fear that they will deny me﴾ (al-Shu'ara'). And how could one who claims divinity listen to a messenger?

It is narrated that in the time of the Caliph al-Ma'mun(1), one man claimed prophethood and they imprisoned him. Then another claimed it, and he said: "Bring the two of them together so that one may confront the other." When they were present, they said: "Sir, this man claims prophethood." He said: "He lies. I have not sent anyone." Thus he made himself a god after having been a prophet.

1 He is Abdullah ibn Harun al-Rashid, Abu al-Abbas, the seventh of the Abbasid caliphs in Iraq and one of the great rulers. Born in the year 170 AH, he was concerned with translating books of philosophy into Arabic, and he gave freedom of speech to researchers and to people of debate and philosophy, except for the ordeal over the createdness of the Qur'an in the last year of his life. He died in the year 218 AH at the age of 48. (al-A'lam 4/142)

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi) on surah 26, verse 13:

Moses continues speaking of his fears:

﴿And my chest tightens, and my tongue is not freed, so send [word] to Aaron﴾ (26:13)

My chest tightens when they call me a liar, and tightness of the chest results in my stammering and becoming tongue-tied, so that I cannot speak persuasive speech. That is because I will witness a clear falsehood confronting a clear truth, and my chest is bound to tighten at that, especially since Moses, peace be upon him, has a precedent concerning the matter of speech.

Therefore he said: ﴿So send [word] to Aaron﴾ (26:13). In another verse: ﴿And my brother Aaron is more eloquent in tongue than I, so send him with me as a helper (ridan) to confirm me; indeed I fear that they will deny me﴾ (28:34).

That is, a helper for me who will speak on my behalf if my tongue fails in speech. This shows his eagerness, peace be upon him, to convey the call of his Lord to Pharaoh and his people.

Accordingly, both Moses and Aaron were messengers, except that the Qur'an said once of them: ﴿Indeed we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ (26:16) in the singular form, and said another time: ﴿Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord...﴾ (20:47) in the dual form.

It is well known that a human being needs food and drink to sustain his life, and before that and more important than it, he needs to sustain his breath. Do you not see that he can endure hunger, and can endure thirst, but he cannot endure at all without air; if inhalation or exhalation is cut off from him, he departs from life?

We have said before that among God's mercy to us is that He lets people own food in abundance and water rarely, but air God does not let anyone own, why?

Because if your enemy owned the air and withheld it from you, you would die before he became pleased with you. In addition, air is the essential element of life, and upon it its movement depends.

We also observe that when a person climbs to a high place (he pants), and his heartbeat and breathing increase, why? Because movement requires much air; if the air decreases, the chest tightens, because it suffices only to sustain life, but it does not suffice for a person's external movement.

¹ Radaʾa (ردأه): he strengthened him and helped him; al-radaʾ (الردء) means the helper and supporter. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/260).

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me﴾ [26:14]:

I wish the matter stopped at the issue of speech between the Prophet of God, Moses, and his people. Rather, there was for him an old grudge, because he had killed one of them, even though it was unintentional, as He, the Exalted, said in another verse: ﴿So Moses struck him and finished him off...﴾ [28:15], "so I fear that they will kill me for it."

(1) The "charge" here is the killing of the Copt, whose name was Fāthūr. Qatadah said: the Copt wanted to conscript the Israelite to carry firewood for Pharaoh's kitchen, and he refused, so he cried out for help to Moses. ﴿So Moses struck him and finished him off...﴾ [28:15]: that is, he pushed him with his palm. Moses, peace be upon him, did that without intending to kill him; he only meant to repel him, but his life was taken by it. (Tafsir al-Qurtubi, 7/5146–5147).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 15:

Then the Truthful (Al-Haqq), glorified is He, says to Musa and Harun:

﴿He said: "Never! So go, both of you, with Our signs. Indeed, We are with you, listening."﴾ (15)

(Kalla) serves to negate what precedes it, and before it there are three matters: ﴿I fear that they will deny me﴾ (12) (ash-Shu'ara'), ﴿and my chest tightens and my tongue is not eloquent...﴾ (13) (ash-Shu'ara'), ﴿and I fear that they will kill me﴾ (14) (ash-Shu'ara'). So, upon which of them does this negation fall?

The negation here is directed at what concerns Musa, peace be upon him, not at the people's denial of him. His Lord says to him: be reassured, for none of all this will happen. The negation does not fall on their denial of him, because he will be denied; therefore we see the precision of the Qur'anic expression, where ﴿I fear that they will deny me﴾ (12) comes at the end of the verse, and after it comes a new statement ﴿and my chest tightens...﴾ (13), which is what is intended by the negation.

Surah al-Fajr has clarified the meaning of (kalla) plainly in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tries him by bestowing honour upon him and blessing him, he says, "My Lord has honoured me." But when He tries him by restricting his provision, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me."﴾ (al-Fajr 15-16)

Then He says after it, in response to it: ﴿Never!...﴾ (17) (al-Fajr). That is: giving is not a proof of honour, nor withholding a proof of humiliation; rather, what is meant is a trial by blessing and by affliction.

And how can the matter be as you suppose, when Allah has given you and you have been miserly, and you love wealth with an abundant love, so you do not spend from it on the orphan or the needy, but rather you compete in gathering it until you devour the inheritance and take people's wealth?

Therefore: the wealth with which Allah honoured you was not a blessing for you, because you made it a curse and a ruin, when you were given and yet withheld.

This word (kalla) has a history with Musa, peace be upon him. He learned it from his Lord and grasped its lesson well. When he and his followers were surrounded, with the sea before them and Pharaoh and his soldiers behind them, until his followers became certain that they would be overtaken and destroyed, Musa, peace be upon him, said it with full conviction: ﴿He said: "Never! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me."﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 62)

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So go, both of you, with Our signs...﴾ (15) (ash-Shu'ara'), the "signs" here mean the miracles that indicate the truthfulness of the two in conveying the message from Allah, and here they are the staff. ﴿Indeed, We are with you, listening﴾ (15) (ash-Shu'ara'), as He said to them in another place: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ (46) (Ta-Ha).

Sometimes He mentions hearing only, and sometimes hearing and seeing. Why? Because his encounter with Pharaoh will at first be argument and debate, and hearing suits this; after that, situations will arise involving (fa'ala) and ('amila) in the matter of magic and the throwing of the staff, and this requires both hearing and sight, because harm may come through hearing alone from the first meeting, and may come through hearing and sight afterward.

1 Qadara Allah al-rizq: He made the provision narrow, in proportion to need, not exceeding the necessity of life. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/102).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 16:

﴿So come to Pharaoh and say: Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds.﴾

It has already been stated, where He (glorified is He) said: ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Pharaoh...﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:10-11]. Here the people of Pharaoh are mentioned first, because they were the cause of his tyranny, when they heard his speech and helped him against (the messengers). Here He says: ﴿So come to Pharaoh...﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:16], because when Pharaoh is defeated, his people who supported him are defeated too. So the discourse here is directed to the pinnacle of disbelief, which is Pharaoh.

﴿Then say: Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:16]. "Inna" (indeed, we) is a plural form that is said of the dual, and despite this, "rasul" (messenger) came in the singular form, and He did not say "rasula" (messengers). This is because the messenger is an intermediary between the one who sends and the one to whom he is sent, whether he is singular, dual, or plural.

Did Moses and Aaron say the word "inna..." [indeed, we] together in one voice? No. Rather, the one of them who was foremost would speak, and the other would listen silently, so that he would be like one who says "amin" to the words of his companion. Do you not see that the Noble Qur'an, when it presented the matter of Moses and his people, clarified that Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and was arrogant... etc.

Until (Moses) prayed against them: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus 10:88].

This is the speech of Moses (peace be upon him), and God responded to him: ﴿Your supplication has been answered...﴾ [Yunus 10:89], using the dual form, although the speaker is one. They said [(1)]: This is because Moses was the one making supplication, and Aaron was saying "amin" to his supplication, and the one who says "amin" is one of the two supplicants and a partner in the supplication.

(1) Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abu Hurayra, who said: "When Moses made supplication, Aaron would say 'amin' to his supplication." He also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas: "Moses supplicated and Aaron said 'amin'." 'Ikrima also said this, as transmitted from him by 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh. (al-Suyuti cited these reports in al-Durr al-Manthur 4/385).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 26, verse 17:

فما مطلوبك يا رسول رب العالمين ؟.
"So what is it that you want, O messenger of the Lord of the worlds?"

﴿أن أرسل معنا بني إسرائيل ١٧﴾ :
﴿That you send with us the Children of Israel.﴾

فالأصل في لقاء موسى بفرعون أن ينقذ بني إسرائيل من العذاب، ثم يبلغهم منهج الله، ويأخذ بأيديهم إليه، وجاءت دعوة فرعون للإيمان ونقاشه في ادعائه الألوهية تابعة لهذا الأصل.
The basic purpose of Musa's (Moses') encounter with Fir'awn (Pharaoh) was to rescue the Children of Israel from torment, then to convey to them the method (manhaj) of God and lead them to it by the hand. The call of Pharaoh to faith and the debate about his claim to divinity came as a consequence of this basic purpose.

وفي موضع آخر :﴿فأرسل معنا بني إسرائيل ولا تعذبهم قد جئناك بآية من ربك... ٤٧﴾( طه )
And in another place: ﴿So send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them. We have come to you with a sign from your Lord...﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:47)

إذن : فتلوين الأساليب في القصص القرآني يشرح لقطات مختلفة من القصة، ويوضح بعض جوانبها، وإن بدا هذا تكرارا في المعنى الإجمالي، وهذا واضح في قوله تعالى في أول قصة موسى عليه السلام :﴿فالتقطه آل فرعون ليكون لهم عدوا وحزنا... ٨﴾( القصص )
So: the variation of styles in the Qur'anic narrative explains different snapshots of the story and clarifies some of its aspects, even if this appears as repetition in the general meaning. This is clear in His saying, at the beginning of the story of Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief...﴾ (al-Qasas 28:8)

وفي آية أخرى يقول تعالى على لسان امرأة فرعون :﴿قرت عين لي ولك... ٩﴾( القصص ) وكأن الله تعالى يقول : ستأخذونه ليكون قرة عين لكم، إنما هو سيكون عدوا.
And in another verse He says, on the tongue of Pharaoh's wife: ﴿A coolness of the eye for me and for you...﴾ (al-Qasas 28:9). It is as if God is saying: you will take him so that he becomes a delight to your eyes, but in truth he will become an enemy.

والله تعالى يقول :﴿واعلموا أن الله يحول(١) بين المرء وقلبه... ٢٤﴾( الأنفال ) ففرعون في حين كان يقتل الأطفال من بني إسرائيل، ويستحي البنات، جاءه هذا الطفل بهذه الطريقة اللافتة للنظر، فكان عليهم أن يفهموا أن من ألقي في التابوت وفي اليم بافتعال، هو بهدف نجاته من القتل، فلو كان فرعون إلها، فكيف مرت عليه هذه الحيلة وجازت عليه ؟.
And God says: ﴿And know that God comes between a person and his heart...﴾ (al-Anfal 8:24)¹ Pharaoh, while he was killing the sons of the Children of Israel and sparing their daughters, was presented with this child in this striking manner. They should have understood that the one who was placed in the chest and in the river by contrivance was aiming at his rescue from killing. So if Pharaoh were a god, how did this trick pass over him and get past him?

وهذا يدل على أن الله تعالى إذا أراد إنفاذ أمر سلب من ذوي العقول عقولهم، وحال بين المرء وقلبه، ويدل على غباء قومه ؛ لأنهم لو تأملوا هذه المسألة لظهر لهم كذب فرعوه في ادعائه الألوهية.
This shows that when God wills to carry out a matter, He strips people of understanding of their minds and comes between a person and his heart, and it shows the stupidity of his people, for had they reflected on this matter, the falsehood of Pharaoh's claim to divinity would have become clear to them.

١ أي: أن الله يملك أن يصرف قلب الإنسان ويغير نيته كما يريد، فالمرء لا يملك قلبه وإنما الله هو الذي يملكه..
¹ That is: God has the power to turn a person's heart and change his intention as He wills; a person does not possess his own heart, rather God is the One who possesses it.

Pharaoh's response to Moses, peace be upon him, was:

﴿He said: Did we not raise you among us as a child, and did you not remain among us for many years of your life?﴾

He wants to remind Moses of what happened during his upbringing in his house for several years, until he grew up and matured, as if he is rebuking him: how can he take this hostile stance toward him after all that had passed between them?

﴿And you remained among us for many years of your life﴾ It is said that Moses stayed in Pharaoh's house until the age of eighteen, or the age of thirty. The meaning is that he raised him and that he also stayed with him for a number of years.

Whoever reflects on this argument, which Pharaoh thinks is in his favor, finds that it works against him and reveals his foolishness. For if he were a god, as he claims, he would have known that his destruction would come at the hands of this child whom he took in and raised.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 19:

﴿And you did your deed which you did, and you were of the ungrateful.﴾

The "deed" (al-fi'lah) is meant as Moses' (peace be upon him) killing of the man whom he struck and who died. ﴿And you were of the ungrateful﴾ may mean: of those who deny the divinity of Pharaoh, or of those who deny Our favour upon you and Our raising you.

Therefore, the wise see that when a person raises children and sees them as he loves, he should know that it is a success (tawfiq) and care from God, the Exalted. The evidence is that children are raised in one environment, and perhaps they are twins, yet you see one of them righteous and the other wicked. So the matter is a divine care over you. One of the poets captured this meaning, saying:

If you do not find in your sons care,
then the hopeful one has lied and the aspirant has failed.
So Moses, whom Gabriel raised, is a disbeliever,
and Moses, whom Pharaoh raised, is a messenger.

The intended Moses here is al-Samiri, the owner of the calf. His mother placed him in a desert and died, so God sent Gabriel (peace be upon him) to care for him and raise him. Such contrasts only come about through the care of God, glory be to Him.

1. Several opinions have been reported on the meaning of this phrase ﴿And you were of the ungrateful﴾:
- That is, in your killing of the Copt, since he was a soul whose killing is not permitted. Said by al-Dahhak.
- That is, by My blessing which was upon us for you, of raising and kindness to you. Said by Ibn Zayd.
- In that I am your God. Said by al-Hasan.
- Of those who disbelieve in God, because you were with us on this religion of ours which you criticise. Said by al-Suddi.
Al-Qurtubi cited these opinions in his tafsir (7/4973).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 20:

﴿Said he, "I did it then when I was among the misguided.™ ﴾ :

Musa (peace be upon him) says: I do not deny that I killed him, but I killed him while I was among the misguided. That is, the ignorant of what the killing would entail, and I never believed at all that this blow would finish off the man.

The word ﴿al-dallin﴾ (al-Shu'ara') here does not mean lacking guidance. From this sense of dalal is the expression "dalla al-tariq" (he lost the way), where one did not intend to go astray; rather, he wandered against his will.

From the same usage is the Almighty's saying concerning testimony: ﴿that if one of them errs, the other can remind her...﴾ (al-Baqarah, 282).

And His saying, addressing His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And He found you wandering, and guided you﴾ (al-Duha, 7). That is: bewildered between the falsehood practised by his people.

And (He) showed the truth that has no need of proof: ﴿So I fled from you when I feared you, then my Lord granted me wisdom and made me among the messengers﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:21).

﴿Wisdom...﴾ (21): that is, [the ability] to place things in their proper places. This word came after ﴿I did it when I was among the misguided﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:20). It is as if he were saying: "I did strike the man; that is true, and he died. This was an unintended error, and I was wronged in it, because God had granted me wisdom and the capacity to place things in their proper place."

And this is not all; rather also:

﴿And made me among the messengers﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:21).

(1) Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (7/4973): "Between the departure of Musa (peace be upon him) when he killed the Copt and his return as a prophet there were eleven years, apart from some months."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 22:

﴿And this is a favour with which you reproach me, that you have enslaved the Children of Israel.﴾

Meaning: it is what Pharaoh threw in Moses' face when he said:

﴿Did we not bring you up among us as a child, and you stayed among us for some years of your life? And you did your deed which you did...﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 18-19).

It is as if he is saying to him: Do you remind me of these things and count this as a kindness, when it is worth nothing compared with what you did, namely enslaving the Children of Israel, slaughtering their sons, sparing their women, and putting them to service in your employ.

The killing of the males and the sparing of the females does not mean mercy toward them; rather, it means humiliation and degradation for them, since the woman finds none of her male kin to protect or defend her, so she remains after the men in humiliation and degradation, in service to Pharaoh.

¹ Al-Dahhak said: the speech came in the form of rebuke (tabkit). Rebuke may take the form of a question or not a question, and the meaning is: had you not killed the Children of Israel, my parents would have raised me, so what favour do you have over me? For you are reminding me of something you ought not to remind me of. Transmitted by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (7/4974).

Then the Truthful, Glorified One says:

﴿Pharaoh said: "And what is the Lord of the worlds?"﴾ [26:23]

That is: "This is a new matter that you have brought, O Moses."

(1) He asked with "mā" (what), a question about an unknown among things. Makki and others said: it is as one asks about kinds (genera), and for this reason he asked with "mā." A question with "man" (who) has also occurred in another place, and it seems that these are occasions (of different usage). (Related by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir, 7/4976).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 24:

Pharaoh asked: "Who then is the Lord of the worlds of whom you speak?"

﴿He said: "The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you were certain."﴾

Because the heavens, with what is in them of planets, stars, the sun, the moon, orbits and constellations, and the earth, with what is in it of seas, rivers, mountains, deserts, plants, animals and humans, had already come into existence before you came into existence, O you, Pharaoh the god! !

So then: he answered him with something that was established in the universe before his coming and before his birth. It is as if the intended meaning for Moses, peace be upon him, is: "Tell me, O Pharaoh, O you who claim divinity, what has your divinity added to the universe? If this whole universe, with its heavens and its earth, belongs to Allah, the Lord of the worlds, then what have you done?"

He did not limit himself to the heavens and the earth, but said ﴿and whatever is between them﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:24), meaning: of air and birds that swim in the open space. They did not know what we know now of the secrets of the air, and of the transmission of sound and image through it. In the atmosphere of the sky, in the space between heaven and earth, there are secrets that deserve reflection.

Then he speaks to them gently, saying: ﴿if you were certain﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:24), meaning: if you were certain that these things were not created except by Allah.

Then Allah, glorified is He, mentions Pharaoh's dispute, saying:

﴿He said to those around him, "Do you not listen?"﴾

Pharaoh says to those around him from among his followers, who had acknowledged his divinity: "Do you not listen to what he says?" He means Musa, peace be upon him. Pharaoh would not say this phrase unless he sensed in his people a satisfaction with what Musa had said, namely the denial of lordship and divinity from Pharaoh and its attribution to Allah, the Exalted, Creator of the heavens and the earth.

Pharaoh was expecting his people to confront what Musa said, to rebuke him and silence him. But nothing of this happened, which indicates that they were wishing that Musa would prevail and that Pharaoh would be brought down, because he had suppressed their freedoms and opinions, and they knew his lie and were awaiting deliverance from him.

This is evidenced by what the Qur'an relates about the believing man (1) from the family of Pharaoh who was concealing his faith, and by those who came later and embellished for him the matter of the magicians while they wished he would be defeated.

(1) Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said: "Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah,' and he has come to you with clear evidences from your Lord? And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie; but if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will strike you..."﴾ [Ghafir 40:28] and the verses that follow.

Before any of Pharaoh's people could respond, Musa (peace be upon him) pre-empted them:

﴿He said: "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old."﴾ [26:26]

Here Musa (peace be upon him) moves Pharaoh from the cosmic scene that surrounds him, in the heavens and the earth and what lies between them, to his own self. He says to him: You had forefathers before you were born and before you claimed divinity. So who was their Lord?

When Musa, peace be upon him, tightened the noose around Pharaoh, Pharaoh wanted to escape this argument and this losing debate, so he said, trying to salvage his position:

﴿He said: "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman."﴾

This statement from Pharaoh exposes the one who made it: he testified that Musa is a messenger, and his own words betrayed him without his realizing it.

Musa (peace be upon him) responds with another proof, but this time he concludes it with his saying ﴿If you have understanding, 28﴾ (al-Shu'ara'). In the previous one he had said ﴿If you are certain, 24﴾ (al-Shu'ara'), as if he is saying to Pharaoh: since things have reached the point where you accuse me of madness, I will not say "if you are certain" but rather "if you have understanding," so he brought the opposite of madness.

Pharaoh brings this debate to an end, and gives his own conclusion of the matter as he sees it, saying:

﴿He said: "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned."﴾

This is from Pharaoh a bankruptcy of argument. Had he had a reply to what Moses was saying, he would have answered him, and would have met proof with proof. Instead, he overpowered his opponent by threatening him with prison and exile, and among them, the one imprisoned would remain in prison until death.

Pharaoh did not take into account, in this matter, the people around him, lest they discover this bankruptcy and this foolishness in his response.

(1) In his saying ﴿لأجعلنك من المسجونين﴾ ("I will surely make you among the imprisoned"), he did not say "لأسجننك" ("I will imprison you"), even though it is more concise. Why? Abu Yahya Zakariya al-Ansari said in his book "Fath al-Rahman bi-Kashf ma Yaltabis fi al-Qur'an" (p. 299): "It is intended to define it as a known category, i.e., 'I will make you among those whose condition I know in my prison.' When he imprisoned a person, he would throw him into a deep, dark pit, where he could neither see nor hear."

Moses, peace be upon him, postpones what he has with him of the signs, and continues in argument and in displaying proof:

﴿He said: "Even if I bring you something clear?"﴾

That is: if you are not convinced by all the proofs given earlier, then if I bring you a clear sign indicating the truth of my message, will you still make me one of those imprisoned?

Look at the contradiction within Pharaoh himself. At the moment he heard these words from Musa, he should have insisted on imprisoning him. But Allah, blessed and exalted is He, wills to make His proof manifest, so He causes Pharaoh himself to demand it personally: ﴿He said, "Then bring it, if you are of the truthful."﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:31). It was not for Musa to bring a sign except that Pharaoh demand it from him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 26, verse 32:

﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a serpent, plainly visible.﴾

The casting down of the staff in the Qur'an has three stages. The first is the one that accompanied God's choosing of Musa to be a messenger, when He said to him: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ (Ta-Ha 17). We have said that Musa, peace be upon him, lengthened his answer to this question out of his eagerness to prolong the intimate companionship with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so he said: ﴿It is my staff; I lean upon it, and I beat down leaves with it for my flock, and I have in it other uses.﴾ (Ta-Ha 18)

So the staff, in Musa's view, peace be upon him, was a piece of wood recently severed from its origin, like a branch on a tree. But with Allah it has another story: ﴿He said, "Throw it down, O Musa." So he threw it down, and behold, it was a snake, moving swiftly.﴾ (Ta-Ha 19–20)

The staff did not become a staff except after it was cut from its tree and lost vegetative life and turned into an inanimate object. Had it returned to its origin and become a tree again, the matter would have been comprehensible. But it passed beyond the rank of the vegetative and turned into the animal, which is the higher rank. Therefore Musa was terrified of it and feared, and his Lord reassured him: ﴿He said, "Take hold of it and fear not; We will return it to its former condition."﴾ (Ta-Ha 21)

This time was in the nature of a training for Musa, peace be upon him, so that he would become accustomed to the staff in this state, as though Allah, Exalted, wished Musa to carry out this experiment before him, so that he would be certain of the truth of this sign. Then, when he met Pharaoh, he would cast it down without fear, being confident of success in this round.

Thus, the second casting of the staff was before Pharaoh and his close circle, and then the casting for the third time was before the sorcerers.

As for the meaning of ﴿plainly visible﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 32): it means clearly a serpent, having life and movement. And [the phrase] ﴿plainly visible﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 32) is also said to mean: evident to all. This is because they [the sorcerers] were skilled in this matter and used to produce illusions for people of such things, making them move and slither. But Musa's staff was not like that; rather it was a serpent, plainly evident, real, and no one could doubt its reality.

Whoever follows the various depictions of this incident in the noble Qur'an finds that the context calls it sometimes "a serpent" (thu'ban), sometimes "a snake" (haya), and sometimes "a jann" (jann). Why? They said: because it combined all these attributes. In the lightness of its movement it is like a jann; in its frightful form it is like a snake; and in its writhing it is like a serpent. And the jann is the young of the snake.

1 Hashsha al-shajar yahushshuhu: he struck the tree with a stick so that its leaves would fall for livestock to eat; the meaning here: I shake down the leaves of the trees with my staff for my flock to eat them (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/303).
2 It is described as: a serpent (thu'ban) in two verses: (al-A'raf 107), (al-Shu'ara' 32). A snake (haya) in one verse: (Ta-Ha 20). A jann in two verses: (al-Naml 10), (al-Qasas 31).

Then the Almighty says:

﴿And draw out his hand, and it came forth white to the onlookers﴾ [33]

Here He speaks of the drawing out of the hand, because He said in another verse: ﴿Insert your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without any defect...﴾ [32] (al-Qasas).

In this way the scenes of one story complete one another, and what some people think to be repetition is not so.

﴿And draw out...﴾ [33] (al-Shu'ara') means: he brought out his hand, ﴿and it came forth white to the onlookers﴾ [33] (al-Shu'ara'), even though Musa (peace be upon him) was dark in complexion, meaning he had some tanning, yet his hand came out white, having a radiance and a sheen that captures the eyes.

Comparing this verse with the verse of surah al-Qasas, we find that the verse of surah al-Shu'ara' omits the jayb (jaib), which is the opening of the garment at the top, not the pocket commonly known today, into which we put money, for example. In the past they would make the pocket inside a person's clothing so that it would be safe; when a person wanted something in it, he would extend his hand through the upper opening of the garment, and so it was called a jayb.

1 Jayb al-qamis (the collar opening of a shirt): that part of it which opens over the chest, i.e., the top of the garment; its plural is juyub (Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/138). So his hand would come out gleaming as though it were a piece of the moon in the brilliance of lightning, without leprosy. And leprosy is a skin disease.

**Surah 26, verse 34:**

﴿He said to the chiefs around him, "Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer."﴾

Al-Mala' (the chiefs): they are the elite of the people, those who fill the eyes (with their dignity) and take the front seats in gatherings. ﴿Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer.﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 26:34] He accused him of sorcery in order to extricate himself from his predicament, and said, "a sorcerer," because Musa had practised this matter only once, the very occasion he performed it before Fir'awn. But the chiefs have knowledge of sorcery and familiarity with it, and among them are many sorcerers.

A distinction is made between sahir (ساحر, sorcerer) and sahhar (سحار, a master sorcerer): sahir refers to one who has practised this act only once, whereas sahhar is an intensive form indicating that it has become his profession, like najir (ناجر, a carpenter/ a worker in wood) and najjar (نجار, a skilled carpenter), and khai'it (خائط, one who sews) and khayyat (خياط, a professional tailor).

And ﴿skilled (ʿalim) [in his sorcery]﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 26:34], i.e., knowledgeable about his sorcery.

He wants to drive you out of your land with his magic, so what do you advise?" (Q. 26:35)

Here Pharaoh summons his people against Musa (Moses) and warns them that he will corrupt the common folk and the masses, that he will gain the majority, and that he will have a faction supporting him against you, so that he drives you out of your land. This is the least that may be expected from him. He wants to incite the chiefs (al-mala') of his people to be enemies to him, standing in the ranks of Pharaoh.

It is strange that Pharaoh, who claims to be a god, says: ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ (Q. 26:35). This is the false divinity that has sunk to the level of slaves. When does a god take the opinion of his slaves, and ask them for help and counsel? Had he been a god in truth, he would have had the solution and the response at hand.

Why did Pharaoh descend from the station of divinity and ask the chiefs of his people for help? They turned their attention to his lie, and found the opportunity favourable for deliverance from him. This shows that most of them and the bulk of them were going along with him reluctantly, waiting for the moment of deliverance from his oppression and his lying. Therefore they said:

﴿They said: "Put him off, him and his brother, and send heralds to the cities ﴾ [Qur'an 26:36]

﴿Arjihi... ﴾ [26:36] from al-irjā' (ارجاء), which means delay: that is, postpone him and his brother for a period. ﴿And send heralds to the cities﴾ [26:36]: send your messengers to gather the sorcerers (al-saḥḥarīn) from all parts of the lands, so that they may confront Moses and Aaron with their sorcery. "Al-madā'in" is the plural of "madīnah" (city).

﴿They will bring you every skilled sorcerer who has knowledge﴾.

He said: ﴿sahhar﴾ [sorcerer], in the intensive form (ṣīghat al-mubālaghah), and ﴿ʿalīm﴾ [knowing], meaning: well-versed in the various arts of sorcery and the tricks of sorcerers.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 38:

﴿So the magicians were gathered for the appointed time of a known day﴾ [26:38]

Al-Mīqāt: that is, the known time. In another verse: ﴿He said, "Your appointment is the day of adornment..."﴾ [20:59]. It was a day witnessed by them, on which the young women would wear their finest garments. It was a festival day on which they would choose the bride of the Nile into whom they would throw [the offering]. So the day was specified, and then the day was not left in its general sense; rather, a time from the day was specified: the forenoon(1) ﴿and that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾ [20:59].

In another scene, the place was specified, and he said: ﴿a place equidistant﴾ [20:58]. That is, it has equality (sawā'iyya): either by the levelness of the place, so that all may be able to see this magical contest, being in an open ground level in its terrain; or it is a place of equal distance, central between the cities from which the magicians would be gathered, so that it is not extreme, such that its attendance would be burdensome for some of them.

Thus the various scenes converge to draw the complete picture of the story.

We see in this counsel the eagerness of the chiefs to complete this encounter, and that it be in the sight of the assembled crowds, because they know that it will be to Moses' advantage, and this encounter will expose the falsehood of Pharaoh's claim to divinity.

1 Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (3/156): "That is: at the forenoon of the day, so that it would be more evident, clearer, more manifest and more apparent."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 26, verses 39–40:

﴿And it was said to the people: "Are you gathering?" ﴾ (39) ﴿"So that we may follow the sorcerers, if they are the victors."﴾ (40)

That is: they began calling the people together, as if they were in a campaign of publicity and support, either for Musa (Moses), from among his supporters who secretly hated Pharaoh, or for Pharaoh. So both these and those were eager to attend this contest.

We see, for example, a vast crowd of spectators gathering to watch a football match. How much more so a contest between sorcerers, who claim divinity, and Musa, who came with a new message, saying that its God is other than this god? It is an event that shook the whole world and drew everyone to witness it.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 26, verses 39–40:

﴿And it was said to the people: "Are you gathering?" ﴾ (39) ﴿"So that we may follow the sorcerers, if they are the victors."﴾ (40)

That is: they began calling the people together, as if they were in a campaign of publicity and support, either for Musa (Moses), from among his supporters who secretly hated Pharaoh, or for Pharaoh. So both these and those were eager to attend this contest.

We see, for example, a vast crowd of spectators gathering to watch a football match. How much more so a contest between sorcerers, who claim divinity, and Musa, who came with a new message, saying that its God is other than this god? It is an event that shook the whole world and drew everyone to witness it.

Then the Truthful One, glorified is He, says:

﴿So when the magicians came, they said to Pharaoh, "Will there truly be a reward for us if we are the victors?"﴾

Look at the course of this "god" Pharaoh among his subjects. The true God feeds and is not fed, He grants protection and is not given protection, He gives and does not take. When the magicians gathered, and they were the champions of this contest, and they knew how much Pharaoh needed them in this situation, they hastened to make an agreement with him and to lay down a condition for him: if you are making people serve you without pay, this matter is different, and it will not pass like this without a reward.

This is evidence of their knowledge of Pharaoh, and that he was a man of appetite (ukulati), so they stipulated a reward from him in case they were the victors. We do not know; perhaps another will come who threatens the lordship, and so we are saving you for just such a situation.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 42:

﴿Qala na'am wa-innakum idhan lamina al-muqarrabin﴾ (42)

Here Pharaoh sets aside his arrogance and haughtiness and acquiesces to the conditions of his magicians, and even gives them more than they asked for. ﴿And indeed, you will then be among those brought near﴾ (26:42). That is, you will be among our inner circle; we will seek your help in such matters and will not dispense with you, because you are the ones who upheld the falsehood of our divinity.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 43:

﴿Said Moses to them: "Throw what you are going to throw."﴾ (43):

Here there is speech that has been omitted, which we know from the context of the story, because the preceding verse still had the speech going on between Pharaoh and the sorcerers. The Qur'an omits some events, relying on the discernment of the listener or reader, as we have said in the story of the hoopoe (hudhud) with Prophet Solomon (peace be upon him), when he said to it: ﴿Take this letter of mine and throw it to them, then turn away from them and see what they return.﴾ (An-Naml, 28)

Then he said after it: ﴿She said, "O chiefs, indeed there has been delivered to me a noble letter."﴾ (An-Naml, 29), and what lies between these two events has been omitted, which we know from the context.

As for His saying ﴿Throw what you are going to throw﴾ (Ash-Shu'ara', 43), this is the goal that was reached after the dialogue with the sorcerers.

1. He means by "noble" (karim): what she saw of his wondrous affair, that a bird came with it and threw it to her and then turned away from her out of courtesy, and this is a matter no king could accomplish. (Tafsir Ibn Kathir 3/361). Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (7/5074): "I described it as such because it included gentleness of speech and admonition in calling to the worship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and good solicitation, without including reviling or cursing or anything that disturbs the soul, and without harsh or obscure speech, in keeping with the custom of the messengers in calling to Allah."

Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 44:

﴿So they threw their ropes and their staffs, and said, "By the might of Pharaoh, we are surely the victors."﴾

So the staffs and the ropes were the instruments of their sorcery. ﴿And they said, "By the might of Pharaoh, we are surely the victors."﴾ (al-Shu'ara). "By the might of Pharaoh": this is their oath, and how wretched an oath it is, for Pharaoh, in their view, is never overcome or subdued. We have already explained that ʿizzah (might, dominance) means being beyond subjugation and not being defeated. But the might of Pharaoh is false might: arrogance and pride without any foundation of right, a might in sin, like the one of which God said: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride in sin takes hold of him...﴾ (al-Baqarah, 206).

God the Exalted also said: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder. Nay, those who disbelieve are in pride and opposition.﴾ (Sad), that is, might in sin and might in falsehood.

From the same root is His saying about the hypocrites: ﴿If we return to Madinah, the mightier will surely expel the weaker from it...﴾ (al-Munafiqun, 8). The Qur'an confirmed their claim that the mightier would expel the weaker, but ﴿to God belongs might, and to His Messenger and to the believers...﴾ (al-Munafiqun, 8).

Since the matter is so, you are the weak, and you are the ones who will be expelled, and so it was.

It is said that the implements of their magic, namely the staffs and ropes, were hollow and they had filled them with mercury. So when they cast them into the light of the sun and its heat, they began to move about as if they were moving. This is among the tricks and deceptions of the magicians, which make the eyes imagine things that are not real. For the reality of a thing is fixed, whereas the one who is bewitched imagines that they are moving. Then He, glorified be He, says:

﴿Then Moses cast down his staff, and behold, it swallowed up what they were falsifying.﴾ [Q. 26:45]

Moses' casting of his staff did not come directly after the magicians had cast theirs. Rather, there were events mentioned in other verses and in other scenes of the story. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Then behold, their ropes and their staffs appeared to him, by their magic, to be moving.﴾ [Q. 20:66]

﴿So Moses felt a fear within himself. We said, "Fear not; indeed, you are the superior. And throw down what is in your right hand; it will swallow up what they have made. What they have made is only the trick of a magician..."﴾ [Q. 20:67-69]

Thus was the scene. When Moses feared, his Lord strengthened him, supported him with the truth and with proof, and followed him moment by moment in what he did, to guide him, to correct his conduct, and to firm up his heart. The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, would not send him and then abandon him. His Lord had said to him before that: ﴿And that you may be brought up under My eye.﴾ [Q. 20:39] and He said: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see.﴾ [Q. 20:46] So Allah, glorified be He, gives His prophet Moses commands, gives him the proof to carry them out, and then follows him with His care and protection.

Among that is His saying to His prophet Noah: ﴿And construct the ship under Our eyes and by Our inspiration...﴾ [Q. 11:37]

When these scenes are gathered together, you find that they encompass the event, and each completes the other. Some think this is repetition, but it is not so.

So, Moses' casting of his staff came after a new directive from Allah during the contest: ﴿And throw down what is in your right hand...﴾ [Q. 20:69]. And here: ﴿Then Moses cast down his staff, and behold, it swallowed up what they were falsifying﴾ [Q. 26:45]. The meaning of ﴿talqaf﴾ (swallows up) is to devour and gobble up swiftly and forcefully. Speed, the compression of time, and strength indicate seizing with intensity and vehemence, and in this is evidence that he entered the contest with strength, so his strength did not weaken when he saw the tricks of the magicians.

The meaning of ﴿ya'fikun﴾ (they falsify) in Q. 26:45 derives from ifk, which means turning realities upside down. Therefore they called lying ifk, because it reverses the truth and alters reality.

Among its uses is ﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down﴾ [Q. 53:53], meaning the wrongdoing towns that Allah destroyed, so He made their highest part their lowest.

We had previously explained that lying and the reversal of realities come from the fact that when you speak, a statement has three relations: a relation in the mind, a relation on the tongue, and a relation in reality. If the verbal relation corresponds to reality, you are truthful; if it contradicts it, you are a liar.

And He called what the magicians do ifk because they alter the reality and make people imagine something other than it.

¹ That is: the cities of the people of Lot, which He overturned upon them, so He made their highest part their lowest, and rained upon them stones of baked clay, layered. Qatadah said: In the cities of the people of Lot there were four thousand thousand people (that is, 4 million), and the valley was set ablaze upon them with some fire, naphtha and tar like the mouth of a furnace. (Tafsir Ibn Kathir 4/259).

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on surah 26, verse 46:

﴿So the magicians were cast down prostrate, (46)﴾

The Truth, glorified is He, did not say "fa-sajada al-saharah" (so the magicians prostrated). Rather, He said ﴿fa-ulqiya al-saharatu sajidin﴾ (so the magicians were cast down prostrate). The word "ilqa'" (casting down) indicates the swiftness of their response, and that the prostration came from them without deliberation, because it was a matter beyond their own will. It is as if the majesty of the situation, its awe, and the marvel of what they saw cast them to the ground, prostrating to Allah, the Lord of this dazzling sign.

Therefore they did not say at that moment, "We believe in the Lord of Moses and Aaron," but rather they said:

﴿They said: "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron."﴾

When we reflect on the reaction of the magicians here, we find that they first fell down prostrating to Allah, and then they declared their faith. It is well known that faith precedes action, and that prostration does not come except after faith. So how is this to be understood?

They said: there is a difference between the occurrence of faith and your reporting about faith. What came later on their part was not the faith itself but the announcement of it, because they did not prostrate except out of a firm faith in which every doubt was dispelled. It was a faith that seized their minds and cast them to the ground prostrate before Allah, so that it did not give them time to declare it. It returned them to the innate faith within the human soul, and matters of innate nature have no cure through thought.

It is as if someone had asked them: "Why are you prostrating?" And they said: ﴿"We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron."﴾

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 48:

They said: "The Lord of Musa and Harun" after "the Lord of the worlds," so as to cut off the way for Fir'awn (Pharaoh) and his followers, lest he say, for instance, "I am the Lord of the worlds." So they removed this ambiguity by their saying: ﴿The Lord of Musa and Harun﴾ (26:48).

An example of this is the saying of Bilqis when she saw her throne in the presence of Sulayman (peace be upon him). She did not say, "I have submitted to Sulayman." Rather, she said: ﴿I have submitted with Sulayman to Allah, the Lord of the worlds﴾ (27:44). So I and you are two Muslims submitting to one God, who is Allah, the Lord of the worlds. This is how the submission of kings is. And lest anyone suppose that she had submitted only to Sulayman, she was careful in her wording to remove this doubt.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 49:

﴿He said: "Do you believe in him before I give you permission? He is indeed your chief who taught you magic. But you will soon know. I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you all."﴾

Thus: he does not doubt that what the magicians saw compels faith, and he does not dispute that, but the whole matter is ﴿before I give you permission﴾ (al-Shu'ara'). He still clings to his divinity and his tyranny, even after his affair was exposed and his lie became clear, and the chiefs believed in the true God.

Then he wanted to justify his position before the common masses, lest anyone say that he was defeated and his prestige was lost, so he said: ﴿He is indeed your chief who taught you magic...﴾ (al-Shu'ara'). Yet the people know that Musa, peace be upon him, never sat throughout his life with a magician. But Pharaoh takes this as a pretext, to salvage whatever can be salvaged of his position that has collapsed, and of his divinity that has been lost.

Then he threatens them in a manner that reveals his agitation, that he has lost his balance and become confused even in his expression, where he says: ﴿But you will soon know...﴾ (al-Shu'ara'). The word "soon" (sawfa) indicates the future, even though he did not delay his threat to them, as is evident from his saying after it: ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you all﴾ (al-Shu'ara'). ﴿On opposite sides﴾ means: the right hand with the left foot, or the left hand with the right foot.

As for his words ﴿and I will surely crucify you...﴾ (al-Shu'ara'), he clarified it in another verse: ﴿and I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees...﴾ (Ta-Ha 71).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 50:

So what was the response of the believers in the Lord of the worlds?

﴿They said: "No harm! Indeed, to our Lord we are returning."﴾

That is: there is no harm upon us if you kill us, because the destiny of all is toward death.
