The hardship of revelation upon the Messenger of God did not subside until revelation had paused from him and was cut off for a period, during which the Messenger of God longed for it and awaited it. After that, there was sent down to him His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast? 1 And We relieved you of your burden 2 which had weighed upon your back 3 And raised for you your repute. 4﴾ (al-Sharh).

And there was sent down to him: ﴿By the morning brightness 1 And by the night when it covers 2 Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He detested [you]. 3 And the Hereafter is better for you than the first. 4﴾ (al-Duha).

That is: the revelation will return to you with ease and without hardship, and you will not tire in receiving it, as you used to suffer before.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Sent down... 193﴾ (al-Shu'ara'), indicates height: that the Qur'an descended from above, from God, not from the composition of a human being who errs and is right, who is ignorant of what is beneficial, as we see in man-made laws that are amended every day, that do not suit the requirements of development, and whose defects appear day after day.

And because the Qur'an descended from above, it is incumbent upon us to receive it as one who trusts in it and is reassured by it, not opposing it and not being arrogant toward it, for you are arrogant toward an equal of yours, whereas what comes to you from above necessitates that you submit to it, by conviction.

In the countryside we hear them saying: "Whoever the Sharia cuts his finger, no blood will flow." Why? Because it has cut by the command of one above you, by the command of God, not by the command of someone like you.

And when we reflect on His saying, exalted is He, in legislating a ruling: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you... 151﴾ (al-An'am).

The word (ta'alaw) (come) means: leave the lowness of earthly legislation and turn to the elevation of heavenly legislation. So ta'alaw means: rise up and ascend; do not descend to the level of the earth, or else you will be exhausted and the events will grip you; for the one who legislates for you is one like you, even if they are well-intentioned, and they do not know the realities of matters. If they are right in one thing, they are wrong in other things, and you will be compelled to change these legislations and amend them. So the safest course for you is to take from above, for He, glorified is He, is the All-Knowing of what benefits you.

Thus: ﴿Sent down... 193﴾ (al-Shu'ara') indicates that it is from above, from the source of goodness. Even iron, which is one of God's blessings, when He spoke of it, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the Balance that people may maintain justice. And We sent down iron, in which is great might and benefits for people, and that God may make evident who supports Him and His messengers unseen. Indeed, God is Powerful and Exalted in Might. 25﴾ (al-Hadid).

He did not say, for example: "We sent down diamonds or pearls, or other precious metals." Why? Because iron is an instrument of supporting the call and proclaiming the word of God.

Gabriel, peace be upon him, was named the Spirit because by the spirit there is life. The angels are living beings, but they have no material substance, so they are as if they were absolute spirits; as for humans, they are matter in which there is a spirit.

Also, the word "spirit" is used in several senses, among them: ﴿And they ask you about the Spirit. Say: The Spirit is of the affair of my Lord... 85﴾ (al-Isra'), and the intended meaning is the spirit by which we live.

And the Qur'an was named a spirit: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit of Our command... 52﴾ (al-Shura). So the Qur'an is a spirit, and the angel who brought it down is a spirit. If you say: "What need do I have for a spirit within a spirit?"

We say to you: this spirit by which your matter lives is the one that departs from you when you die, and the matter ends. As for the spirit that comes to you in the Qur'an, it is an enduring, eternal spirit; it is the method of God that gives you the everlasting life that does not end.

Therefore, the spirit by which matter lives is shared by the believer and the disbeliever alike, but the spirit that comes to you from the Book of God and in His method is specific to the believer; it endures, and by it a new, eternal life is resumed after the life of perishable matter.

And recite, if you wish, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, respond to God and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life... 24﴾ (al-Anfal).

How so, when we are alive? Yes, we are alive by the first spirit, the spirit of perishable matter. But the Messenger of God calls us to the enduring life, as if He, Mighty and Majestic is He, is indicating that this life we live is not the true life, because it will end, and there is another life that is lasting and everlasting.

Even our saying "we are alive" is an exaggeration, for the living are those who do not die, and this life comes only through the method of God. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, the Hereafter is the [true] life, if they only knew. 64﴾ (al-Ankabut). So "al-hayawan" is an intensification of life, that is, the true life; as for the life of matter, what kind of life is it in which a person dies on the day of his birth, or even after a hundred years?!

Then the Truthful, glorified and exalted is He, describes the Spirit as ﴿the Trustworthy 193﴾ (al-Shu'ara'), that is, over the revelation. The Qur'an, therefore, is protected with God, protected with the Trustworthy Spirit who brought it down, protected with the Trustworthy Prophet to whom it was sent down.

Therefore He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And if he had made up about Us some sayings, 44 We would have seized him by the right hand, 45 Then We would have cut from him the aorta. 46 And not one of you could have prevented Us from him. 47﴾ (al-Haqqah).

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And he is not, over the unseen, [one who is] withholding. 24 Nor is it the speech of an accursed devil. 25﴾ (al-Takwir).

1 Narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, that he used to say: "When revelation came down upon the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, there was heard near his face a humming like the humming of bees." Recorded by Ahmad in his Musnad (1/34).

2 Al-Bukhari mentioned in his Sahih, Book of Prayer, chapter on what is mentioned about the thigh (12), the statement of Zayd ibn Thabit, scribe of the revelation, may God be pleased with him, as a mawquf report: "God sent down revelation upon His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, while his thigh was on my thigh, and it became so heavy upon me that I feared my thigh would be crushed" (Fath al-Bari 1/478). Ibn Hajar said: it is a fragment of a hadith connected in al-Bukhari in the tafsir of Surat al-Nisa', regarding the revelation of His saying: ﴿Not equal are those who sit [at home] among the believers... 95﴾ (al-Nisa') (recorded by al-Bukhari in his Sahih, 4592).

3 From Asma' bint Yazid, who said: "I was holding the reins of al-Adba', the she-camel of the Messenger of God, when there was sent down to him the entire Surat al-Ma'idah, and it nearly broke the shoulder of the she-camel from its weight." Recorded by Ahmad in his Musnad (6/455).

4 Al-Watin: a vein in the heart which, if severed, causes its owner to die; it is the main vital artery that supplies the body with pure blood flowing from the heart. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then We would have cut from him the aorta 46﴾ (al-Haqqah), meaning: We would have ended him swiftly and destroyed him quickly if he opposed Our command in any way. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/319).

5 Al-Danin: the miser. He, glorified is He, does not withhold any unseen matter from the Messenger of God, but conveys to him everything God has revealed to him of news from heaven. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/396).

Then the Almighty says:

﴿Upon your heart, that you may be among the warners.﴾ [26:194]

Did the Qur'an descend upon the ear of the Messenger of Allah, or upon his heart? The ear is the instrument of hearing, yet Allah says ﴿upon your heart﴾ (26:194), because the ear is a passageway to the heart, which is the seat of reception. The heart is the "dynamo" (the driving power) of movement in the human body: by the blood it pumps into the organs and systems of the body, energies and the capacity for movement and for performing functions are generated.

Thus, for example, we see a patient take medicine by mouth, and the medicine travels the course of food and is absorbed slowly. If you wish the medicine to reach the body quickly, you give an injection into the muscle; but faster than this is to give an injection into the vein, so that it mixes directly with the blood and takes effect in the body rapidly. Blood is the means of life in the human soul.

Therefore the heart is the place of reflection and contemplation, and hearing by the ear has no value if the heart does not comprehend what the ear hears. For this reason He, glorified is He, says in another place: ﴿Say: whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, for he has brought it down upon your heart...﴾ (2:97).

The meaning is: he brought it down upon your heart directly, as if it did not pass through the ear. For Allah the Exalted chose for this task a messenger whom He fashioned under His own eye, and removed from him the human obstacles that hinder this directness. So the heart of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, became alert to receive the speech of Allah, because it was fashioned under the eye of Allah. As for those who heard the speech of Allah with their ears but did not respond to it, their hearts were closed and hard, so they did not understand.

The heart is the locus of obligations and the abode of beliefs, and to it ends the outcome of all the means of perception: the eye sees, the ear hears, the nose smells, the hands touch... then all of this is presented to the intellect to choose among the alternatives. When the intellect chooses and is at rest with a proposition, it conveys it to the heart so that it may settle there. That is why we call it a "belief" (ʿaqīdah), meaning a matter over which the heart has tied its knot (ʿaqd), so that it no longer floats up to the intellect to be examined anew. It has become firmly rooted in the heart and has become a fixed belief.

In many verses the reliance and the focus is upon the heart. Allah says: ﴿It is not their flesh nor their blood that reaches Allah, but it is piety from you that reaches Him...﴾ (22:37).

In another verse He shows that piety has its seat in the heart: ﴿That, and whoever honours the rites of Allah, indeed it is from the piety of hearts﴾ (22:32).

And concerning testimony He says: ﴿And do not conceal testimony, for whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful...﴾ (2:283), even though testimony is by the tongue, not by the heart.

Therefore the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, says in the hadith narrated by al-Nu'man ibn Bashir: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart." (1)

The Companions of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, tell us that revelation would descend upon him with many verses amounting to two-quarters or three-quarters of [a portion] at one time. When he, peace and blessings be upon him, was relieved of it, he would say: "Write." Then he would recite them to them, placing each verse in its place within its surah. Then he, peace and blessings be upon him, would recite them in the prayer, and they would be exactly as he had dictated them to them. That is because the Qur'an had touched his heart, not merely his ear.

Out of his eagerness to preserve the Qur'an, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would repeat it after Gabriel and reiterate it so that he would not forget it. So Allah revealed to him:(2) ﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ (87:6).

And He said in another place: ﴿Do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you, and say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ (20:114).

And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recital. So when We have recited it, follow its recital. Then indeed, upon Us is its explanation﴾ (75:16-19).

Among the wondrous aspects of the Qur'an is that you will not find a person who utters a speech for, say, five minutes, then repeats it to you verbatim as he said it. Yet the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would have a surah recited to him, and he would repeat it exactly as it was. This is from His saying: ﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ (87:6).

As for His saying: ﴿that you may be among the warners﴾ (26:194). The warner (mundhir) is one who warns against evil before it occurs, so that the listener may take precaution and not fall into the causes of evil. Warning does not benefit at the moment the evil has already happened, for in that case it is of no use. Likewise, glad tidings of good are given before it occurs, to urge the listener toward good and to spur him to it.

He, glorified is He, says in another verse: ﴿That you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned...﴾ (36:6).

Just as the messengers before warned their peoples, so you warn your people, and join the procession of the messages.

(1) A hadith agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayh), narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (2051), and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (1599), and Ahmad in his Musnad (4/270-274), from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, whose opening is: "Indeed the lawful is clear, and indeed the unlawful is clear."

(2) From Ibn ʿAbbas: when Gabriel brought the revelation to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, he would not finish until he was overcome by it, so the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would begin speaking its opening words out of fear that he would faint. Gabriel said to him: "Why do you do that?" He said: "Out of fear that I will forget." So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ (87:6). Narrated by al-Tabarani in his al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (12649), and cited by al-Haythami in Majma' al-Zawa'id (7/136), where he said: "In it is Jubayr, and he is weak," and likewise al-Suyuti weakened it in Asbab al-Nuzul (p. 296).

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿In a clear Arabic tongue.﴾ [26:195]

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿In a clear Arabic tongue﴾ (al-Shu'ara'). If the Qur'an was sent down upon your heart, then how do they hear it and memorize it? Here comes the role of the Arabic tongue, which brings the Qur'an out to the people. Thus, the speech of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) comes after its descent upon the heart, and the tongue comes after it, because it is the means of memorization, preservation and recitation.

The meaning of ﴿clear﴾ (mubin) [26:195] (al-Shu'ara') is: plain and evident, encompassing all the affairs of life. But someone may say: if the Qur'an was sent down in the Arabic tongue, then what about non-Arabic words that it uses? For example, qistas is Roman (Byzantine), amin is Abyssinian, and sijjil is Persian.[1][2]

We say: the meaning of "Arabic tongue" is what the Arabs spoke and what circulated on their tongues, because it became part of their language and became Arabic, even if it originally came from other languages. What is meant is that it did not bring a new speech unknown to the Arabs; before the Qur'an was sent down, these words were already common in the Arabic tongue.

The Qur'an was sent down in the Arabic tongue specifically, because the Arabs are the nation that receives the call and carries it to the rest of the nations, so they must understand the Qur'an. If you say: the other non-Arab nations are also addressed by this Arabic Qur'an, so how will they receive it and understand it? We say: whoever among the Arabs hears it must convey it in the tongue of the people he calls, and this is our duty as Arabs toward the Book of God.

1. Al-Firyabi related from Mujahid, who said: "Qistas: justice in Roman (Greek)." It was also related by Ibn Abi Hatim from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "Qistas in the language of the Romans: the balance." (al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an by al-Suyuti, 2/115).
2. Al-Firyabi related from Mujahid, who said: "Sijjil is Persian. Its first part is stones and its last part is clay." (al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an by al-Suyuti, 2/112).

**Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 196:**

﴿And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the former peoples.﴾ (196)

The pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ (indeed it/he) may refer to the Qur'an, as does the preceding reference, and it may refer to the Messenger of Allah. The word ﴿zubur﴾ is the plural of ﴿zabur﴾, meaning written and inscribed. If the minds that opposed the Messenger of Allah, denied his message and denied his miracle had only reflected on the earlier revelations directly before him, namely Judaism and Christianity in the Torah and the Gospel, they would have been obliged to believe him, because he is mentioned in the books of the former peoples.

As Allah, glorified is He, said in another place: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures, the scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾ (87:18-19).

The general principles of beliefs, morals, divine justice and the stories of the prophets are all established matters found in all books and with all the prophets. Only the legal rulings differ from one scripture to another, to suit the age and the time in which each came.

When you read His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion that which He enjoined upon Noah and that which We revealed to you and that which We enjoined upon Abraham and Moses and Jesus, saying, "Establish the religion and do not be divided therein..."﴾ (42:13)

you may say: Then why was the Qur'an revealed, and why did He not say "that which We enjoined upon Muhammad"?

They said: Because the rulings would change, to suit all the ages for whose guidance the Qur'an was revealed, and all places, and to suit the universality of Islam.

It is therefore narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam (1), and another man named Ibn Yamin, who were from the People of the Book, and both testified that they saw the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ) in the Torah and in the Gospel. The Qur'an says of them: ﴿They recognise him as they recognise their own sons...﴾ (2:146)

When Ibn Salam heard it, he said: "Our Lord has been lenient with us in this matter. By Allah, I recognise him as I recognise my own son, and my recognition of Muhammad is stronger" (2).

Allah, the Exalted, says in this meaning: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel...﴾ (7:157)

And He, glorified is He, says on the tongue of Jesus, peace be upon him, when he stood preaching to his people: ﴿And a messenger who comes after me, whose name is Ahmad...﴾ (61:6)

So: ﴿And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the former peoples﴾ (26:196), that is, Muhammad (ﷺ), or the noble Qur'an; both are correct, because the attributes of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) are present in these books, or the Qur'an is in the general outlines of its principles of beliefs, morals, resurrection and the lives of the prophets.

Thus it was obligatory upon those to whom the Qur'an came to believe in it, especially since the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was unlettered, having never sat with a teacher, and his history in this regard is known to them, as he had never before read or written anything.

The Qur'an affirms this matter, saying, addressing His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿You did not recite before it any scripture, nor did you write one with your right hand; otherwise the falsifiers would have had doubt﴾ (29:48).

﴿You were not residing among the people of Madyan, reciting to them Our verses, but We were sending [the message]﴾ (28:45)

﴿You were not on the western side when We conveyed to Moses the command...﴾ (28:44)

﴿You were not with them when they cast their pens, [to see] which of them would take charge of Mary...﴾ (3:44)

All these verses and others are evidence that he (ﷺ) had no knowledge of them except through direct revelation in the noble Qur'an, and it was incumbent upon the people to believe in him at the first moment they heard it.

(1) He is ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam ibn al-Harith al-Isra'ili, Abu Yusuf, a Companion who embraced Islam when the Prophet (ﷺ) arrived in Medina. His name had been al-Husayn, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named him ʿAbd Allah. He witnessed with ʿUmar the conquest of Bayt al-Maqdis. He remained in Medina until he died in the year 43 AH (al-Aʿlam of al-Zirikli 4/90).

(2) Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (1/194): "al-Qurtubi said: It is narrated from ʿUmar that he said to ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam: Do you recognise Muhammad as you recognise your son? He said: Yes, and more. The trustworthy one descended from heaven to the trustworthy one on earth with his description, so I recognised him. As for his mother, I do not know what she did."

(3) Thawa bi'l-makan: he settled in the place, remained there and resided in it. The meaning: you were not staying among them (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/113).

Then the Truthful One, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Or was it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel knew it?﴾ (1) [26:197]

Ayah (sign): i.e., a proof and an indication that the Qur'an is from Allah. For the scholars of the Children of Israel used to seek victory through it over those who disbelieved. So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it. Or did they not say to the Aws and the Khazraj in Madinah: "The time of a Prophet has drawn near; we will follow him and slay you with him, O polytheists, as the people of 'Ad and Iram were slain"? (2) Nevertheless, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, they denied him and disbelieved in him, while they knew that he was true. Why?

They said: Because they perceived that he would strip them of leadership. They were in Madinah people of knowledge, people of the Book, people of insight, and people of war... etc. On the night the Prophet (ﷺ) emigrated to Madinah, they were preparing to crown 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy as king over it. When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to it, he spoiled this matter for them; therefore they envied him for this station, for he had taken from them the temporal authority that had been theirs.

And the phrase ﴿the scholars of the Children of Israel﴾ [26:197] is used because they knew the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and because he (ﷺ) brought things that only they knew. Five of them became well known: 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, Asad, Usayd, Tha'labah, and Ibn Yamin.

(1) Ibn Sa'd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ataa al-'Awfi: "They were five: Asad, Usayd, Ibn Yamin, Tha'labah, and 'Abd Allah ibn Salam." (Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 6/323).

(2) From elders of the Ansar, who said: "We had dominated them by force for a long time in the Jahiliyyah, and we were people of shirk while they were people of the Book. They would say: 'A Prophet is about to be sent now; we will follow him, his time has drawn near, and we will slay you with him as the people of 'Ad and Iram were slain.' But when Allah sent His Messenger from Quraysh and we followed him, they disbelieved in him." Mentioned by Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir (1/124), citing Ibn Ishaq.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And if We had sent it down upon some of the non-Arabs, [198] and he had recited it to them, they would not have been believers in it. [199]﴾

We have indeed sent down the Qur'an in a clear Arabic tongue, to an Arab nation; and had We sent it down to the non-Arabs (a'ajam), they would not have understood it.

And the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, says in another place: ﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said, "Why are its verses not explained in detail? Is it non-Arabic and [the messenger] Arabic?" Say, "It is, for those who believe, a guidance and a healing. And those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is for them a blindness. Those are being called from a distant place."﴾ (Fussilat [41:44]).

Why? Because the receptive faculty is closed. If you wish to receive any matter, you must first clear your heart of any other matter that opposes it; then, after that, you may study the two matters, and whatever agrees with the truth, admit it.

Therefore He, exalted, says: ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body…﴾ (al-Ahzab [33:4]). So it is one heart; therefore remove from it every prior matter. Behold, the Qur'an is one, its speaker is one, its conveyor is one, and its tongue is Arabic.

He, exalted, describes their state upon hearing the Qur'an: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, some of them look at others, [saying], "Does anyone see you?" Then they turn away. Allah has turned their hearts away because they are a people who do not understand.﴾ (al-Tawbah [9:127]). That is, they intend to slip away and leave.

And He says in another verse: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, among them are those who say, "Which of you has this increased in faith?"…﴾ (al-Tawbah [9:124]). That is: what did it benefit you, and what did it add to your faith?

And He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you until, when they leave from your presence, they say to those who were given knowledge, "What did he just say?" Those are the ones upon whose hearts Allah has set a seal, and who have followed their desires.﴾ (Muhammad [47:16]). Meaning: what is the new thing he has brought?

And He says concerning those who believe: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety.﴾ (Muhammad [47:17]). The word ﴿a'ajamin﴾ (الأعجمين, "non-Arabs") in verse 198 of al-Shu'ara' is the plural of a'jam (أعجم), and the a'jam is one who does not speak Arabic well even if he pronounces it; ajami is the opposite of Arabi, and al-'ajam are non-Arabs. So the meaning of ﴿And if We had sent it down…﴾ (al-Shu'ara' [26:198]) is: the Arabic Qur'an, if sent down upon some of the non-Arabs, they would not have understood it. He said ﴿some (بعض)﴾ to allow for possibility: among the non-Arabs there are those who learned Arabic and mastered it, and so can understand the Qur'an.

1 Qatadah said: He means: If We had sent down this Qur'an upon some of the non-Arabs, the Arabs would have been the most intense of people against it, not understanding it and not knowing what it is. Recorded by 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim.
- Qatadah also said: If Allah had sent it down non-Arabic, they would have been the most losing of people by it, because they do not know the non-Arabic tongue. Recorded by 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir. (Both cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 6/323).
2 Ibn 'Abbas said, as recorded by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim: they are the hypocrites. (Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 4/326).
3 Ibn Jurayj said: The believers and the hypocrites used to gather around the Prophet (ﷺ); the believers would listen to what he said and retain it, and the hypocrites would hear it but not retain it. When they left, they would ask the believers, "What did he just say?" Then there was revealed: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you…﴾ (Muhammad [47:16]). Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (7/466) and attributed to Ibn al-Mundhir.

And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So he recited it to them, they would not have believed in it﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:199]. That is because they did not understand anything from it. Likewise, you are like these non-Arabs in receiving and taking in the speech of God; they did not understand anything from it.

That is because they loved disbelief and obstinacy and persisted in it, and their hearts found rest in it until they became infatuated with it. So God helped them in it, and sealed their hearts, so that no faith enters them and no disbelief leaves them.

The meaning of ﴿We have inserted it...﴾ (Surah al-Shu'ara', 26:200): We made it enter into the hearts of the criminals, as if they were *ajam* (non-Arabic speakers) who do not understand anything of it.

Therefore: ﴿They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment﴾ (Ash-Shu'ara' 26:201). And since they will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment, their faith will not be accepted from them.

The meaning of ﴿suddenly, while they do not perceive﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:202) is: unexpectedly, and from where they do not perceive.

Therefore, when the Qur'an was revealed and some of the Companions believed in the Messenger of Allah, the Messenger of Allah and his Companions were persecuted and harmed, until they no longer felt safe from the tyranny of the disbelievers. They would spend the night armed and wake up armed, finding no one to protect them.

In this state, the words of the Exalted were revealed: ﴿The multitude will be put to flight and they will turn their backs﴾ (al-Qamar 54:45). Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, was astonished: "What multitude is this that will be defeated, when the Muslims are in this condition?" But when he witnessed Badr and what took place there of the killing of the polytheists and the victory of the religion of Allah, he said: "Yes, Allah has spoken the truth: the multitude will be put to flight and they will turn their backs."(1)

1 Ibn Kathir cited it in his tafsir (4/266) and attributed it to Ibn Abi Hatim, from Ikrimah, who said: "When ﴿The multitude will be put to flight and they will turn their backs﴾ (al-Qamar 54:45) was revealed, Umar said: 'What multitude will be defeated? What multitude will be overcome?' Umar said: 'When the day of Badr came, I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) leaping in his armor while saying: "The multitude will be put to flight and they will turn their backs." Then I understood its interpretation on that day.'"

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 203:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿So they will say, "Are we to be reprieved?" Then do they seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾

That is: "Give us respite and be patient with us, and postpone the punishment from us. Glory be to God! Did you not seek to hasten it?" This is the nature of the people of obstinacy and disbelief: if We leave them, they ask that it be sent down upon them; and if the punishment descends upon them, they say, "Give us respite and be patient with us."

(1) He, exalted is He, says about them: ﴿And they said, "Our Lord, hasten for us our share [of punishment] before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ (Surah Sad 38:16). That is: hasten for us the punishment. And He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment, and had there not been a specified term, the punishment would have come to them. And it will surely come upon them suddenly while they are unaware. They ask you to hasten the punishment, and indeed Hell encompasses the disbelievers.﴾ (Surah al-Ankabut 29:53-54).

Meaning: "Give us respite and be patient with us, and delay the punishment from us. Glory be to God! Did you not used to seek to hasten it?" And this is the nature of the people of obstinacy and disbelief: if we leave them, they ask that it be sent down upon them, and if the punishment descends upon them, they say, "Give us respite and be patient with us."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 205:

Then the Lord of Might, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Have you considered: if We give them enjoyment for years,﴾ [205] ﴿and then there comes to them what they were promised,﴾ [206] ﴿what they were given enjoyment of will not avail them.﴾ [207]

﴿Have you considered...﴾ [205] (al-Shu'ara') means: tell Me. ﴿If We give them enjoyment for years [205] and then there comes to them what they were promised [206]﴾ (al-Shu'ara'). Despite the length of the period, the end is one.¹ ﴿What they were given enjoyment of will not avail them [207]﴾ (al-Shu'ara').

¹ Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (7/5021): "The intended people are the people of Makkah, according to the view of al-Dahhak and others."²

² That is: even if We delay them, grant them respite, and give them a long time of the age and a period of time, however long it is, and then the command of Allah comes to them, what use will the enjoyment they were in be to them? (Tafsir Ibn Kathir 3/348).

﴿Have you considered...﴾ 205. That is: tell me. ﴿If We let them enjoy for years,﴾ 205 ﴿then there comes to them what they were promised,﴾ 206 and despite the length of the period, the end is one.¹ ﴿What they had been enjoying did not avail them at all.﴾ 207

﴿Have you considered...﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:205): meaning, "Tell me," ﴿if We let them enjoy for years﴾ (26:205), ﴿then there comes to them what they were promised﴾ (26:206), ﴿all that they had been enjoying would not avail them﴾ (26:207).

Despite the length of the period, the end is one and the same (1): ﴿all that they had been enjoying would not avail them﴾.

(1) That is: even if We delayed them, gave them respite, and granted them a span of time, a long or short while, and then the command of God came upon them, what availed them of the bounty they were in? (Tafsir Ibn Kathir, 3/348).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 208:

﴿And We did not destroy any town except that it had warners [sent to it] – as a reminder. And We were never unjust.﴾

As Allah, Glorified is He, says in another verse: ﴿That is because your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are unaware.﴾ (al-An'am), for a messenger had come to them, teaching them and warning them, in order to establish the proof against them, as Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger.﴾ (al-Isra').

ذِكرى... ٢٠٩ (الشعراء): This is all a reminder — we mention it to awaken your heedlessness. ﴿وَمَا كُنَّا ظَالِمِينَ﴾ (الشعراء ٢٠٩): "And We were not wrongdoers." You are the ones who did this to yourselves. ﴿وَمَا ظَلَمْنَاهُمْ وَلَٰكِن كَانُوا أَنفُسَهُمْ يَظْلِمُونَ﴾ (النحل ١١٨): "And We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves."

The Most High then says concerning the Qur'an:

﴿The devils have not brought it down. It does not befit them, nor are they able to do so.﴾

Because they said: "The devils only brought down the Qur'an upon Muhammad." They would say this of every poet who was skilled in his poetry among them, for every poet has a devil who dictates poetry to him. Among them there was a valley called "Abqar" (ʿAbqar), which is the valley of the jinn, and they would say: "So-and-so is ʿabqarī," meaning: connected to the jinn in this valley.

But how can that be, when the Book that was revealed to Muhammad is an enemy of the devils, cursing them on every occasion and warning its followers against them: ﴿The Shaytan promises you poverty and commands you to indecency...﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:268), and the Most High says: ﴿Indeed, Shaytan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his party that they may be among the companions of the Blaze.﴾ (Fatir 35:6)

So how, then, would the Shaytan support him and dictate to him, when he is his enemy? And why would he not come to you, when you are his beloved ones? This is the first point.

*A repeated passage, since it shares [its subject] with verse 210. Then the Exalted says about the Qur'an:*

﴿The devils have not brought it down. It is not suitable for them, nor are they able to do so.﴾ (26:210–211)

Because they said: "The devils only descended upon Muhammad with the Qur'an." They used to say this about every poet skilled in poetry among them. Each poet, they claimed, had a devil who dictated poetry to him. They had a valley called "Abqar" (Abqar), which is the valley of the jinn. They would say, "So-and-so is *'abqari*" (a term of genius, meaning excellent), that is, connected to the jinn in this valley.

But how could that be, when the Book sent down upon Muhammad is an enemy of the devils? It curses them on every occasion and warns its followers against them: ﴿The Satan promises you poverty and commands you to indecency...﴾ (2:268, al-Baqarah). And the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his party that they may be among the companions of the Blaze.﴾ (35:6, Fatir)

So how, then, would Satan supply the Qur'an and dictate it to him, when Satan is his enemy? And why would he not come to you, when you are his friends? That is one point.

The other: ﴿It is not suitable for them, nor are they able to do so.﴾ (26:211, al-Shu'ara'). God made the Qur'an a miracle and a method, and a miracle cannot be dominated by human or jinn so that they corrupt it. Therefore He, glorified be He, said: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian.﴾ (15:9, al-Hijr)

As for the earlier books, their followers were asked to preserve them. There is a difference between preservation by Me and a request for preservation from you, because a request is a obligation, and it is liable to be obeyed or disobeyed. We have tested the preservation by humans, and they did not safeguard their earlier books. Therefore the Exalted, may He be glorified and exalted, took upon Himself the preservation of His Qur'an personally and did not entrust it to any of His creation.

For this reason you find in this field many wonders and paradoxes. With the passage of time and the overwhelming dominance of civilizations hostile to Islam, which rain upon us every day with torrents of deviations and departures from the teachings of the religion, and some of us are swept along behind them, all of this diminishes the rulings of Islam that are applied.

Yet despite all this, you find the Qur'an becoming ever more documented, ever more preserved, and non-Muslims competing in memorizing the Book of God, documenting it, and innovating in its printing, until we have seen a copy of the Qur'an on a single sheet of paper, and a copy the size of a finger joint, and some of them now boast that they own the smallest Qur'an in the world... etc., regardless of their motives behind this.

The important point is that God, the Exalted, makes even the enemies of the Qur'an serve its preservation: ﴿And none knows the soldiers of your Lord except Him, and it is not but a reminder to mankind.﴾ (74:31, al-Muddaththir)

Is it not among the means of spreading the Qur'an and preserving it the recording devices and the sound amplifiers that broadcast the words of God everywhere? And no earlier book has received such care.

So then: the care for the Qur'an as a text does not match the deficiency in the application of its rulings and the neglect of them by its people. It is as if God, Mighty and Majestic, is saying to us: "I will preserve this text through those who do not believe in it, and I will make them document it and care for it, so that this becomes a proof against you."

For this reason, before the World War, the Germans had a cabinet with drawers, and in each drawer there was a verse of the Qur'an, in which was kept everything written about that verse from the tafsir of Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with him) up to that time. This is evidence that they are made to serve by a hidden power that none can control except God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian.﴾ (15:9, al-Hijr)

We have previously said that some women walk in the streets with their chests uncovered, yet they adorn their chests with a copy of the Qur'an. Would that they covered their chests and did not hang the Qur'an on them.

So how can you say it was brought down by devils, when the Qur'an came to proclaim to its people its enmity toward them and to warn against them? How, when the devils only descend upon every sinful disbeliever, and you are more deserving of their descent upon you? ﴿Indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you...﴾ (6:121, al-An'am)

And the meaning of ﴿nor are they able to do so﴾ (26:211, al-Shu'ara') is that this matter is beyond their capabilities, because the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, they are from hearing removed.﴾ (26:212)

I translate the passage as given. The text begins mid-commentary, with the verse cited as 26:212, and the quoted verses are from Surah al-Jinn.

The Almighty has explained this meaning in His saying: ﴿And that we touched the heaven, and found it filled with strong guards and flaming meteors. And that we used to sit therein in positions for hearing. But whoever listens now will find for himself a watching flame.﴾ (al-Jinn)

(1) On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah decrees a matter in the heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain upon a smooth rock. When the fear is removed from their hearts, they say: 'What has your Lord said?' They say: 'The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.' Then the eavesdropper (mustaraq al-sam') hears it, and the eavesdroppers are stacked one above another—Sufyan described it with his palm, bending it and spreading its fingers—so one hears the word and conveys it to the one below him, and then that one conveys it to the one below him, until it reaches the tongue of the sorcerer or the soothsayer. Sometimes the meteor overtakes him before he can convey it, and sometimes he conveys it before the meteor reaches him, and he tells a hundred lies along with it." Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (4701, 4800) and Ibn Majah in his Sunan (194).

Then, after that, he speaks about the reception of this method by the Messenger, by his family and followers, and by all the believers:

﴿So do not invoke another god along with Allah, lest you be among those punished.﴾ [26:213]

The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, addressed His Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, saying: ﴿So do not invoke another god along with Allah...﴾ [26:213]. Was the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, at risk of invoking another god along with Allah? They say: No. What is meant is the initiation of guidance and the initiation of obligation. It is as if He were saying to him: Let it be your foundation that you do not take another god along with Allah. It does not mean that the Messenger had taken another god, so that revelation came to forbid him. Rather, it is the beginning of legislation and obligation. And if the great Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, is warned by Allah should he wish to take another god, then what of those who are beneath him?

When the people hear this address directed to the Prophet who was sent to them, they must listen to it and beware of the warning it contains, just as if the head of a state directed an order to the prime minister, for example—and to Allah belongs the highest likeness—and warned him of the consequence of disobeying it. Without doubt, those subordinate to him among the officials will be more obedient to this order.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 214:

﴿And warn your closest kinsmen.﴾

Thus the command passed from the Messenger of Allah to his household and his closest kinsmen, so that the others among his people would be reassured. He commands them only in a matter that he himself is not exempt from. So the first thing he obligates is himself, then his kinsmen, and this is more conducive to obedience and acceptance. For you reject my command if I order you to do something and do not do it myself, but when I order you and go ahead of you in the action, [you accept].

Thus our master ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, was on the pulpit addressing the people and saying: "O people, listen and obey!" A bedouin stood up and said: "There is no hearing for you nor obedience!" Look at this boldness, toward whom? Toward ʿUmar, while he is on the pulpit. ʿUmar said to him: "And why?"

He said: "Because your garment is longer than ours." Cloth was distributed equally among the Muslims, with no distinction between tall and short. So ʿUmar said to his son ʿAbdullah: "Stand up, O ʿAbdullah, so that the people can see you." ʿAbdullah stood and said: "My father is a tall man" (an exaggeration of height), "and his garment from the Muslims' share was not enough for him, so I gave him my garment and he joined it to his own. And here I am before you in my patched cloak." Then the bedouin said: "In that case we hear and we obey."(1)

But where is the example in our departments and government offices today? Where is the director who comes, sits at his desk at eight in the morning, so as to be an example to his subordinates? Among the gravest of the trials we suffer is that we lack exemplary leaders and officials. Therefore, the first thing that legislation and obligation were directed at was the Messenger of Allah and his closest people, his nearest kin; for corruption comes first from the circles of kinship and the entourage surrounding a person. A leader or ruler may be good, but his entourage is the cause of corruption, as they exploit his name for their corruption, or mislead him and blind him to the facts... etc.

Thus, when our master ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, wished to establish something for the nation, knowing that he was strict with them, he would gather his family first and say to them: "I wish to establish such and such. Whoever among you opposes me in any part of this, I will make him an example for all the Muslims." In this way he secured his household and relatives first, and began with them in implementing what he wanted for the Muslims.

Reflect on ﴿And warn your closest kinsmen﴾ (al-Shuʿara'). Warning (indhar), as we have mentioned, is cautioning against evil before its time. He did not say "give glad tidings to your kinsmen," as if to say: beware lest gentleness and tenderness, or compassion for their kinship to you, seize you; rather, begin with them.

The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, complied with this instruction. He would say to his relatives: "O ʿAbbas, O uncle of the Messenger of Allah! O Safiyya, aunt of the Messenger of Allah! O Fatima, daughter of Muhammad! Work (for salvation), for I cannot avail you anything against Allah. People will not come to me with their deeds while you come to me with your lineages."(2)

(1) From al-Hasan: ʿUmar addressed the people while he was caliph, wearing a waist-wrap that had twelve patches. And from Anas: there were three patches between the shoulders of ʿUmar. (Cited by Ibn al-Jawzi in Sifat al-Safwa 1/147.)

(2) From Abu Hurayra: When Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed ﴿And warn your closest kinsmen﴾ (al-Shuʿara'), the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, stood up and said: "O assembly of Quraysh" (or words to that effect), "buy yourselves back, for I cannot avail you anything against Allah. O Banu ʿAbd Manaf, I cannot avail you anything against Allah. O ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, I cannot avail you anything against Allah. O Safiyya, aunt of the Messenger of Allah, I cannot avail you anything against Allah. And O Fatima, daughter of Muhammad, ask me for whatever you wish of my wealth, I cannot avail you anything against Allah." Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (2753), and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (206).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 215:

While He commands him to warn his closest kinsfolk, He says in contrast to that:

﴿And lower your wing to the believers who follow you, [26:215]﴾

After commanding him to be firm with his family and relatives, He commands gentleness and lowering the wing to the rest of the believers who follow him. Lowering the wing is a metaphor for kindness and gentleness in dealing with others, and this meaning is taken from the bird when it bends over its chicks and gathers them under its wing.

Lowering the wing is a sign of tenderness, not of humiliation and submission. By contrast, we say, "So-and-so spread out his wings" when he becomes arrogant and domineering, and you say, "So-and-so has lowered his wing to me" when he disobeys your orders. [Note: the Arabic "مجنح لي" is rendered here as it stands in the text.]

In another place: ﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾ [15:88] (al-Hijr).

And He said regarding the two parents: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy...﴾ [17:24] (al-Isra'). So we do not say: be humiliated before them; rather, be merciful to them and compassionate toward them, for in this lies your honor and your deliverance.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 216:

﴿فإن عصوك فقل إني بريء مما تعملون ٢١٦﴾

If your close relatives disobey you, then do not hesitate to declare it: ﴿Indeed, I am free of what you do.﴾ (al-Shu'ara') At that point you do not observe toward them the right of kinship or the right of close family ties, because they have no right (over you). Therefore He said ﴿Say...﴾ (al-Shu'ara') and did not say "disassociate yourself from them," because one may disassociate from them privately, between himself and them.

But the Truth, blessed and exalted, wants the Messenger of God to declare it before the assembly, so that everyone may know it. Here our Lord teaches us a lesson, so that we do not show partiality to anyone, or flatter him because of his kinship or his station, so that the affairs of life may be set right.

What corrupts our lives and spreads chaos and indifference among us is that we practise hypocrisy and flatter leaders and officials, cover up their transgressions, and treat them with leniency and mercy. All of this undermines the morale of society and invites chaos and laxity.

Therefore Islam teaches us to declare it openly: ﴿Say: Indeed, I am free of what you do.﴾ (al-Shu'ara') so that the law may take its course, so that everyone stands equal before it, and if the offender knows that he will become a lesson to others, he will be deterred.

It is therefore said of 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) that he ruled the whole world, but the truth is that he first ruled himself, and so the world was ruled for him. Likewise, whoever wishes to rule the world in every time and place must first rule himself, so that none of his followers dares to oppose him; and when people see him as an exemplar, they submit to him with hearing and obedience.

Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 217:

﴿And rely upon the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [26:217]

It may be said: "If you do this, my helpers will diminish and my followers and entourage will scatter from around me." We say to you: beware lest you think that they bring you any benefit or ward off any harm from you. The whole matter is in the hand of Allah, the Exalted, and by His command. So it is better for you to be mindful of Allah and to rely upon Him.

﴿And rely upon the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:217]: "the Mighty" is the One who overcomes and is not overcome, who subdues and is not subdued; and despite that, He, glory be to Him, is Merciful to you and to them. The attribute of mercy here negates what some imagine: that might (ʿizza) here entails tyranny (jabarut), subjugation (qahr), or injustice. He, glory be to Him, is merciful in His might, for the might of the Mighty over the arrogant is a mercy toward the one who is arrogant toward Him.

It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, is instructing His vicegerent (khalifa) on earth, especially the ulil-amr (those in authority) among them, teaching him to be shrewd and sincerely advising. He says to him: beware of relying upon a servant like yourself when you are unable to act, for he is incapable just as you are. Since the matter is so, rely upon the Mighty, the Merciful, for His might and His mercy are for you.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 26, verse 218:

﴿Who sees you when you stand (up)﴾ (1) ﴿218﴾ and your movements among those who prostrate ﴿219﴾.

That is: rely upon the One who loves you, who knows your work and your worship when you stand. The meaning is that you stand for Him, may He be glorified, at night while people are asleep, ﴿and your movements among those who prostrate﴾ (Ash-Shu'ara'). From this we understand that it is valid for you to stand (in prayer) alone at night.

His saying ﴿Who sees you when you stand﴾ (Ash-Shu'ara') means: He sees your state in this standing, and what you are upon of joy, and quickness in responding to the call of God in His saying "Allahu Akbar" (God is greatest). He sees you when you stand in a state of an opened heart, turning to God, and eagerness for worship, not in a state of laziness and sluggishness.

If you turn to God, He gives you of the overflowing bounties that compensate you for the gains of this world and its trade, should you leave them to answer the call. Therefore the emblem of the adhan (call to prayer), which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) approved, is (Allahu Akbar), i.e., greater than anything else. If you are in sleep, then God is greater than sleep; if you are in trade, then God is greater than trade; if you are in work, then God is greater than work... and so on.

It is strange to see someone prefer work over prayer on the pretext that the time is long and that prayer can be performed after work ends. This is a feeble argument, because when your Lord calls you (Allahu Akbar), He wants you to respond immediately, not later. Otherwise, how would the response to the call be named if it is delayed beyond its time? The length of time, especially between dawn and noon and between night prayer and dawn, does not mean that you should pray throughout this entire period, because the call requires haste and response.

We have a note on (Allahu Akbar): "akbar" is a comparative form (af'al tafdil) indicating intensification, and instead of "akbar" we would say "kabir" (great). It is as if it points to the fact that work and striving are not a trivial or worthless matter; rather they are great and deserve attention, because they are the sinew of life, and affairs of building up the earth are not upright except by them.

However, if work is great, then God is greater. Your Lord, may He be exalted, does not make you renounce work or renounce the world, because He created it in this form and made work within it to have a role. If you wish, read: ﴿And when the prayer is ended, disperse in the land and seek of God's bounty...﴾ (10) (Al-Jumu'ah).

He said in another place: ﴿And do not forget your share of the world...﴾ (77) (Al-Qasas), because the movement of life is what helps you to perform the prayer and to worship God; by it you sustain yourself, by it you gain strength, and by it you cover your nakedness. What the obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory. Nevertheless, God's call to you has priority in being put first and in being answered first, because He who created you and created it has called you (Allahu Akbar).

(1) Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (3/352): "i.e., He is attentive to you," and he cited sayings, among them:
- That is: when you stand to pray. Said by Ibn 'Abbas.
- He sees your standing, bowing and prostration. Said by 'Ikrimah.
- He sees you when you pray alone. Said by al-Hasan al-Basri.
- He sees you when you rise from your bed or your place of sitting. Said by al-Dahhak.
- He sees you standing, sitting and in your (various) states. Said by Qatadah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 26, verse 219:

And ﴿your turning about among those who prostrate﴾ (al-Shu'ara') means: sitting, standing, bowing and prostrating. Your Lord sees you in all these states, and He sees your joy at standing before Him. So when you put your trust in Him, you deserve that your Lord be mighty and merciful toward you.

Or: the meaning of ﴿And your turning about among those who prostrate﴾ (al-Shu'ara') is that the Prophet (ﷺ) would see his companions praying behind him, so he would see those behind him just as he sees those in front of him, and this was one of the special qualities of the Prophet (ﷺ) (2).

For this reason, he would warn them not to precede him in prayer in bowing, prostrating, standing or sitting, and he would warn them against doing in prayer behind him what is not valid for one praying, relying on the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) does not see them.

1 Mujahid and Qatadah said: "Your turning about among those who pray." Ibn 'Abbas said: "That is, in the loins of the fathers, Adam, Noah and Abraham, until He brought him forth as a prophet." Both are mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (7/5024).

2 On the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in prayer one day, then turned away and said: "O so-and-so, will you not perfect your prayer? Does the one praying not look to see how he prays? For he is only praying for himself. By Allah, I truly see behind me just as I see in front of me." Related by Muslim in his Sahih (423), and al-Nasa'i in his Sunan (2/119).

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ (26:220)

Commentary: "The All-Hearing of what is said, the All-Knowing of what passes through the thoughts."

The Qur'anic verses are rendered in the required format, and the commentary is translated faithfully.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 26, verse 221:

﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend? ۲۲۱ They descend upon every lying sinner. ۲۲۲﴾

It has already been said of the Qur'an that the devils have descended with it. To this it is replied: Come, let me inform you upon whom the devils descend, and let me correct for you this false information. It is true that the devils do descend, but they do not descend upon Muhammad (ﷺ), because he is their enemy. They descend only upon their allies.

The Truthful One, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And indeed the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you...﴾ (al-An'am, 6:121)

Verse 222 of Surah al-Shu'ara' (26): ﴿Upon every lying sinner they descend.﴾ So this is what suits the devils and pleases them. The jinn are of two kinds: among them are the righteous and those who are not righteous, and these are the ones they call the devils (shayatin).

The word ﴿afak...﴾ (lying, from ifk, "falsehood") is an intensive form in falsehood, meaning one who turns realities upside down. These [devils] would snatch news, saying something that may happen to coincide with the truth, and then they would add to it much falsehood.

The hearing is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and its instrument is the ear. So the meaning is: they lend their ears to listening (yulqūna l-sam‘). As in His saying:

﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is a witness.﴾

That is, he lends his hearing so that he may listen, like one who is eager to catch what is said in a low voice, leaning toward it in order to hear it from him. And His saying:

﴿And most of them are liars.﴾

Because some of them, a few, may speak the truth in order to wrap up their lie and cover it over, so you take their truth on this occasion as evidence that they are truthful, while they mix true reports with many false ones.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 224:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And the poets—the deviators follow them.﴾ [26:224]

Al-shu'ara' (the poets) is the plural of sha'ir (poet), who is one who composes poetry, which is measured and rhymed speech. The disbelievers accused the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of being a poet, and the Noble Qur'an refuted them in several places, among them His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe.﴾ [69:41]

It is strange that the disbelievers of Makkah, who were Arabs, people of language, eloquence and expression, and experts in measured and rhymed speech, to the extent that they would establish markets for poetry at Dhu al-Majaz, Dhu al-Majannah and 'Ukaz, and would hang their finest poems on the curtains of the Ka'bah, yet still could not distinguish between poetry and the style of the Noble Qur'an.

So, they knew the difference, but by their saying, as the Qur'an relates it: ﴿Or do they say, "A poet, we await for him the misfortunes of time."﴾ [52:30], they intended by "poetry" the sweet speech that captivates the soul and influences the emotions, even if it is prose. This is what the advocates of free verse call for today, because they compose what they call poetry, but it is neither measured nor rhymed.

The meaning of ﴿al-ghawun﴾ (the deviators) [26:224] is the plural of ghawi, which means the astray, and these are the ones who follow the poets. This is because they support their doctrine in life with the poems they recite; and because their logic is not governed by a principle or a morality, rather their whims govern principle and morality. So if they like something, they praise it, and if they dislike it, they condemn it.

The evidence for this is: ﴿Have you not seen that they wander in every valley, and that they say what they do not do?﴾ [26:225–226]

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 26, verse 225:

﴿Have you not seen that they wander in every valley, 225 And that they say what they do not do? 226﴾

The pronoun in ﴿that they... 225﴾ (al-Shu'ara') refers to the poets. The "wadi" (valley) is the low ground between two mountains, which was a place of travel, of growth of trees and gardens, and of the settling of water.

﴿They wander 225﴾ (al-Shu'ara'). One says: so-and-so wandered (hama) on his face, meaning he went without guidance, without any aim or purpose. The meaning of ﴿in every valley they wander 225﴾ (al-Shu'ara') is that this is the condition of the poets, for they are people of speech and imagination. One of them praises you if he hopes for your goodness, but if you do not give him, he turns to blame you and becomes inventive in harming you. He has no specific valley in which he travels, nor a principle to which he adheres, like one who wanders aimlessly in every valley.

Al-Mutanabbi(1), who is among the greatest poets of the Abbasid era and is proverbial for wisdom and eloquence, is known for his famous verse:
"The horse, the night, and the desert know me,
the sword, the lance, the paper, and the pen."

Once, during one of his journeys, highway robbers came upon him. When he wanted to flee, his servant said to him: "Are you not the one who said:
'The horse, the night, and the desert know me,
the sword, the lance, the paper, and the pen'?"
So he was ashamed to flee, and he stood firm before them until they killed him(2). Before he died he said: "Only this slave killed me." This verse became famous in Arabic literature as the verse that killed its author.

When al-Mutanabbi came to Egypt, he praised its ruler Kafur al-Ikhshidi(3), seeking his favor. Kafur was a black man, which is why he was given the kunya Abu al-Misk. When al-Mutanabbi praised him while he was pleased, he said of him:
"Father of every good thing, not merely Father of Musk."

In another poem he says:
"God has decreed, O Kafur, that you be a lord,
and no judge would deny that you have a equal."

When Kafur did not give him what he sought, and relations between them soured, he satirized him, saying:
"I show you contentment, were the soul to conceal what it conceals,
yet I am not content with myself, nor with you.
Untrustworthiness, breach of promise, treachery, baseness and cowardice(4),
are you a person who appeared to me, or a disgrace?
Your two feet in the sandal please me, though I saw you a man with a sandal, even if barefoot.
Such as you is brought from a distant land
to make laugh the mourning women who wail.
Were it not for the excess of people, I would have come to you praising
you with what I held within myself as satire against you."

A poet may also be stingy, yet he praises generosity and the generous, and raises him to the heavens:
"Whenever you come to him, squinting(5) toward the light of his fire,
you will find the best fire and the best hearth there."(6)

Al-Hutay'a(7), despite his well-known stinginess, praises one of them and describes him with rare generosity, to the point that he was about to slaughter his son for his guest because he found nothing to slaughter. Al-Hutay'a composed in praise of generosity this poem, or poetic story, which is counted among the finest of Arabic poetry; nevertheless, he took no lesson from what he said, and he remained in his withholding and stinginess.

Al-Hutay'a says in describing the generous man:
"Hungry for three nights, his belly bound, covered with sand,
in a desert where no dweller has left a trace.
A brother of his, in whom there is a loneliness of intimacy,
sees misery in it, and from its harshness, blessings.
He isolated in a ravine an old woman beside them,
three shadows, you would think them ...
barefoot and naked, they did not go out for bread baked in ashes,
nor did they know generosity since they were created, nor greed."
He saw a shape in the midst of the darkness and it frightened him.
When he saw a guest, he girded himself and became concerned,
so his son, upon seeing him, said: "O father, slaughter me and prepare food for him,
and do not excuse yourself with poverty against what he thinks of us, that we have wealth, so that it may widen for us the blame."
While they were both thus, a wild she-ass appeared from afar,
arranged behind her young male herd leader in order.
Thirsty, wanting water, she flowed toward them,
upon which she was thirsty for her own blood.
He let her wait until her thirsty ones were satisfied,
and sent into her from his quiver an arrow.
She fell, a fat she-ass with a young one,
full of flesh and filled with fat.
Good tidings to him when he dragged her toward his people,
and good tidings to them when they saw her wound bleeding.
They spent the night generous, having fulfilled the rights of their guest,
having incurred no debt, though they had gained spoils.
Their father spent the night glad at his guest,
and the mother, in her joy, was a mother to him."

And the Mighty God has spoken the truth: ﴿That they wander in every valley 225 And that they say what they do not do 226﴾ (al-Shu'ara'). They describe generosity while they are stingy, and courage while they are cowards, etc.

Once, there gathered before the Prophet ﷺ two poets: al-Zibriqan ibn Badr, Qays ibn 'Asim, and 'Amr ibn al-Ahtam. One of them said two statements praising one of those present as the chief of the tribe. The one praised became angry and saw that this was little regarding his right, and said: "By God, O Messenger of God, he knows of me more than what he said" — meaning: he did not give me my due. The poet said: "As for God, since he has said what he said, he is indeed narrow in giving, foolish in his father, base in his paternal and maternal uncles." Glory be to God! At the beginning of the gathering he was the chief of his tribe, and now he is narrow in giving, foolish in his father, base in his paternal and maternal uncles!!

Then he said: "By God, O Messenger of God, I did not lie in the first, and you have spoken truly in the second" — meaning: I am right in both statements. "But when I was pleased, I said the best I knew, and when I was angry, I said the worst I knew." Then our master the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Indeed, some eloquence is magic."(14)

1 He is Ahmad ibn al-Husayn al-Kindi, Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi. He was born in Kufa in a quarter called "Kinda" in the year 303 AH, and grew up in Syria. He moved about at first seeking literature, the Arabic language and the days of the Arabs. He claimed prophethood in the desert of al-Samawa (between Kufa and Syria), then repented and retracted his claim. He praised Sayf al-Dawla ibn Hamdan and Kafur, then satirized him because he did not appoint him (see al-A'lam of al-Zirikli 1/115).
2 Al-Mutanabbi was killed, together with his son and his servant, at al-Nu'maniyya in the year 354 AH, when Fatik ibn Abi Jahl al-Asadi confronted him on the road with a group of his companions, and al-Mutanabbi also had a group with him. The two parties fought, and al-Mutanabbi was killed near Dayr al-'Aqul (on the western side of the Sawad of Baghdad). This Fatik was the maternal uncle of Dabba ibn Yazid al-Asadi al-'Ayni, whom al-Mutanabbi satirized in his famous rhyming-ba' poem (al-A'lam of al-Zirikli 1/115).
3 Kafur ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ikhshidi, Abu al-Misk, a well-known amir. He was an Abyssinian slave whom al-Ikhshidi, ruler of Egypt (in the year 312 AH), bought, and he was named after him; he freed him, and he rose in rank under him. His ambition continued to raise him until he ruled Egypt (in the year 355 AH). He was born in the year 292 AH and died in Cairo in 357 AH at the age of 65 (al-A'lam of al-Zirikli 5/216).
4 Al-Main: lying.
5 A'shu: to look. It is said: "'ashawtu ila al-nar" when you direct your gaze intently toward the fire. Abu 'Ali al-Qali said so in al-Amali (1/149). Ibn Manzur said in al-Lisan regarding the meaning of the verse: "meaning, when you come to it, you cannot make out its fire because of the weakness of your sight."
6 Cited by Abu 'Ali al-Qali in "al-Amali" (1/149), likewise Ibn Manzur in Lisan al-'Arab (root: '-sh-a), attributing it to al-Hutay'a. Likewise cited by Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani in "al-Aghani" (1/237).
7 He is Jarwal ibn Aws ibn Malik, a mukhadram who lived in both the pre-Islamic and Islamic periods. He embraced Islam, then apostatized. He was nicknamed al-Hutay'a for his shortness and nearness to the ground. He was of evil nature and foolishness, and would affiliate himself with each of the Arab tribes when he was angry with another (al-Aghani of Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani 1/222).
8 Al-Ta'wi: the hungry; mursal: one whose food has mixed with sand. Al-Rasm: the trace.
9 Khubz mulla: bread placed in hot ashes, which are heated so that the bread is buried in them to cook.
10 Ra'ahu: frightened him and alarmed him.
11 'Anat: appeared. 'Ana: the wild asses, from the wild donkeys. Al-Mishal: the leader of the herd.
12 Nahus: fat and full. Tabaqat shahman: became filled with fat and flesh.
13 Al-Kalm: the wound. Yadama: bleeding blood. (See Lisan al-'Arab.)
14 This hadith with this story was narrated by al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwa (5/316) with two chains: the first is broken (munqati') from Muhammad ibn al-Zubayr al-Hanzali, and the second is connected (mawsul) through the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Qays ibn 'Asim, al-Zibriqan ibn Badr, and 'Amr ibn al-Ahtam, the Tamimites, sat with the Messenger of God ﷺ. Al-Zibriqan boasted, saying: "O Messenger of God, I am the chief of Tamim, the one obeyed among them, the one who responds; I protect them from injustice and take their rights for them, and this man knows that," meaning 'Amr ibn al-Ahtam. 'Amr ibn al-Ahtam said: "He is severe in his eloquence, defending his side, obeyed in his own ears." Al-Zibriqan ibn Badr said: "By God, O Messenger of God, he knows of me other than what he said, and nothing prevented him from speaking except envy." 'Amr ibn al-Ahtam said: "I envy you. By God, you are base in your maternal uncles, a source of wealth, foolish in your children, neglectful in your clan. By God, O Messenger of God, you spoke truly in what you said first, and I did not lie in what I said last, but I am a man who, when pleased, says the best I know, and when angry, says the worst I find. You spoke truly in both the first and the last." The Prophet ﷺ then said: "Indeed, some eloquence is magic. Indeed, some eloquence is magic."

Repeated text, as it shares [the verse] with verse 225: "Have you not seen that they wander distractedly in every valley, and that they say what they do not do?" (26:225–226)

The pronoun in "that they [anhum]..." (al-Shu'ara' 225) refers to the poets. The "wadi" (valley) is the low ground between two mountains; it was the place of travel and the place where trees and gardens grew and water settled.

"Yahimun" (al-Shu'ara' 225): we say, "So-and-so wandered (haama) on his face," meaning he went without guidance, without aim or purpose. The meaning of "in every valley they wander" (al-Shu'ara' 225) is that this is the condition of the poets, for they are people of speech and imagination. One of them praises you if he hopes for your goodness, but if you do not give him, he hurls blame at you and becomes inventive in attacking you. He has no specific valley in which he walks, nor a principle to which he holds, like one who wanders aimlessly in every valley.

Al-Mutanabbi(1), who is among the greatest poets of the Abbasid era and is proverbial for wisdom and eloquence, is known for his famous verse:
"The horse, the night, and the desert know me,
and the sword, the lance, the paper, and the pen."

When, on one of his journeys, highwaymen came upon him, and when he wanted to flee, his servant said to him: "Did you not say:
'The horse, the night, and the desert know me,
and the sword, the lance, the paper, and the pen'?"
He felt ashamed to flee, so he stood firm before them until they killed him(2). Before he died he said: "None killed me but this slave." This line became famous in Arabic literature as the verse that killed its author.

When al-Mutanabbi came to Egypt he praised its ruler Kafur al-Ikhshidi(3), hoping for his gifts. Kafur was a black man, so they gave him the kunya Abu al-Misk. When al-Mutanabbi praised him while content, he said of him:
"Father of every good thing, not merely Father of Musk."

In another poem he says:
"God has decreed, O Kafur, that you are the lord,
and no judge can see that you have a second."
But when Kafur did not give him what he sought, relations between them soured, and he satirized him, saying:
"I would show you contentment, if I concealed what is hidden in the soul,
but I am neither content with myself nor with you, O liar(4), breaker of promises, treacherous, base, and cowardly.
Is it a person I see, or disgraces?
Your feet in shoes please me, for I have seen you with shoes even when barefoot.
Someone like you is brought from distant lands
to make the mourning women laugh as they weep.
Had it not been for people's excess talk, I would have come to you praising,
but with what I held within myself, I came to you satirizing."

Sometimes a poet is miserly, yet he praises generosity and the generous, raising him to the heavens:
"Whenever you come to him, seeking by the light of his fire(5),
you will find the best fire and the best hearth there(6)."

Al-Hutay'a(7), despite his well-known stinginess, praises a man and describes him with rare generosity, to the point that he resolved to slaughter his own son for his guest because he had nothing else to slaughter. Al-Hutay'a composed in praise of generosity this poem or poetic tale, which is counted among the finest of Arabic poetry; yet he took no lesson from what he said and continued in his tightfistedness and miserliness.

Al-Hutay'a says in describing the generous man:
"Hungry for three nights, belly bound, with dust-mixed food,
in a desert where no resident has left a trace.
A brother whose harshness holds loneliness,
where he sees misery as blessings from his fierceness.
He left alone on a hill an old woman before him,
and three shadows that you would take for...
barefoot and naked, they had not tasted baked bread,
nor known kindness since they were created.
He saw a figure in the midst of darkness, and it frightened him,
then when he saw a guest, he hurried and was concerned,
and his son said, seeing him bewildered:
'O father, slaughter me and prepare food for him,
and do not excuse yourself by having nothing, for he thinks we have wealth, so he will spare us blame.'
While they were thus, a wild ass appeared from afar,
standing in a line behind its leader.
Thirsty, wanting water, it flowed toward them,
though its thirst would lead it to its own blood.
He let it wait until its thirst was quenched,
and shot an arrow from his quiver into it.
So it fell toward them, a fat she-ass with a young foal,
heavy with flesh and thick with fat.
Good news for him when he dragged it toward his people,
and good news for them when they saw its wound flowing with blood.
They spent the night generous, having fulfilled their guest's right,
and they incurred no debt, though they gained spoils."
"Their father spent the night glad with his guest,
and the mother with her joy as a mother."

As God the Mighty has spoken: "That they wander in every valley, and that they say what they do not do" (al-Shu'ara' 225–226). They describe generosity while they are miserly, and courage while they are cowards, etc.

Once, two poets gathered with the Prophet ﷺ: al-Zibriqan ibn Badr, Qays ibn Asim, and Amr ibn al-Ahtam. One of them spoke two statements praising one of those present as the chief of the tribe. The one praised became angry, seeing this as little regarding his due, and said: "By God, O Messenger of God, he knows of me more than what he said" — meaning: he did not give me my right. The poet said: "As for God, since he has said what he said, he is indeed narrow in giving, foolish in his father, base in his paternal and maternal uncles." Glory be to God! At the start of the assembly he was the chief of his tribe, and now he is narrow in giving, foolish in his father, base in his uncles!!

Then he said: "By God, O Messenger of God, I did not lie in the first, and you have spoken truly in the second" — meaning: I am right in both statements. "But when I was pleased, I said the best I knew, and when I was angry, I said the worst I knew." Then our master, the Messenger of God ﷺ, said: "Indeed, some eloquence is magic"(14).

1. He is Ahmad ibn al-Husayn al-Kindi, Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi, born in Kufa in a quarter called "Kinda" in 303 AH, raised in Syria. He first traveled seeking literature, grammar, and the lore of the Arabs. He claimed prophethood in the badiya of al-Samawa (between Kufa and Syria), then repented and withdrew his claim. He praised Sayf al-Dawla ibn Hamdan and Kafur, then satirized the latter because he did not appoint him (see al-A'lam of al-Zirikli, 1/115).
2. Al-Mutanabbi, his son, and his servant were killed at al-Nu'maniyya in 354 AH, when Fatik ibn Abi Jahl al-Asadi met them on the road with a group of his companions; al-Mutanabbi also had a group, the two sides fought, and al-Mutanabbi was killed near the monastery of al-Aqul (on the western side of the Sawad of Baghdad). This Fatik was the maternal uncle of Dabba ibn Yazid al-Asadi al-Ayni, whom al-Mutanabbi satirized in his well-known Ba'iyya qasida (al-A'lam, 1/115).
3. Kafur ibn Abd Allah al-Ikhshidi, Abu al-Misk, a famous amir. He was an Abyssinian slave bought by al-Ikhshidi, ruler of Egypt (in 312 AH), and was named after him; he was freed and rose in his service. His ambition kept rising until he ruled Egypt (in 355 AH). He was born in 292 AH and died in Cairo in 357 AH at the age of 65 (al-A'lam, 5/216).
4. Al-Ayn: lying.
5. A'shu: to look. It is said: "I 'ashawt toward the fire" when you fix your gaze upon it. Abu Ali al-Qali said so in al-Amali (1/149). Ibn Manzur in Lisan al-Arab said regarding the verse: "That is, when you come to it, you cannot make out its fire because of the weakness of your sight."
