6. Cited by Abu Ali al-Qali in al-Amali (1/149), and likewise by Ibn Manzur in Lisan al-Arab (root 'sh-w), attributing it to al-Hutay'a; also cited by Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani in al-Aghani (1/237).
7. He is Jarwal ibn Aws ibn Malik, a mukhadram who lived in both the Jahiliyya and Islam; he embraced Islam then apostatized. He was called al-Hutay'a for his shortness and nearness to the ground. He was full of evil and foolishness, and he would attach himself to each of the Arab tribes when angry with another (al-Aghani of Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani, 1/222).
8. Al-Tawi: the hungry. Murmal: whose food is mixed with sand. Al-rasm: the trace.
9. Khubz mulla: bread placed in hot ashes that are heated so the bread is buried in them to bake.
10. Ra'ahu: frightened him and startled him.
11. Anat: appeared. Ana: the wild asses, among wild donkeys. Al-Mishal: the leader of the herd.
12. Nahwas: fat and full. Tabaqat shahman: filled with fat and flesh.
13. Al-Kalm: the wound. Yadama: bleeding blood (see Lisan al-Arab).
14. This hadith with this story was narrated by al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwa (5/316) with two chains: the first is broken (munqati') from Muhammad ibn al-Zubayr al-Hanzali, and the second is connected (mawsul) through a hadith of Ibn Abbas, who said: Qays ibn Asim, al-Zibriqan ibn Badr, and Amr ibn al-Ahtam, the Tamimites, sat with the Messenger of God ﷺ. Al-Zibriqan boasted, saying: "O Messenger of God, I am the chief of Tamim, the one obeyed among them, the one who protects them, prevents injustice, and secures their rights. This man (meaning Amr ibn al-Ahtam) knows this." Amr ibn al-Ahtam said: "He is indeed strong in his sides, protective of his flank, obeyed in his ears." Al-Zibriqan said: "By God, O Messenger of God, he knows of me other than what he said, and what prevented him from speaking was only envy." Amr said: "I envy you. By God, you are base in your maternal uncles, a talker of wealth, foolish in your children, wasteful in your clan. By God, O Messenger of God, you spoke truthfully in what you said first, and I did not lie in what I said last, but I am a man who, when pleased, says the best I know, and when angry, says the ugliest I find. You spoke truly in both the first and the last." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, some eloquence is magic; indeed, some eloquence is magic."

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, makes an exception from these deviators:

﴿Except those who believe, do righteous deeds, remember Allah often, and defend themselves after they have been wronged. And those who have done wrong will come to know what a [dreadful] return they will be returned to.﴾

Some of the poets of the polytheists, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zibaʿrā and Musāfiʿ al-Jumaḥī, used to satirize the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and disparage him, and the misguided deviators would gather around them, encouraging them and urging them on to further satire of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Concerning these people was revealed the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the poets—the deviators follow them﴾ (al-Shuʿarāʾ). The poets of Islam then hastened to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawāḥa, Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr, Kaʿb ibn Mālik and Ḥassān ibn Thābit, and they said: "Are we among these, O Messenger of Allah?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited to them this verse:

﴿Except those who believe, do righteous deeds... 227﴾ (al-Shuʿarāʾ).

So the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, made an exception of those poets in whom these four qualities were found: ﴿except those who believe, do righteous deeds, remember Allah often, and defend themselves after they have been wronged... 227﴾ (al-Shuʿarāʾ). That is: they remember Allah in their poetry, so as to alert people to the spiritual raptures of religion and the admonitions of faith, that they may heed them; then they defend the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) against those who satirized him.

These three [and the fourth] used to defend Islam and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): whenever the disbelievers satirized him, they replied to them, refuted their arguments, and defended the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So much so that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set up a pulpit (minbar)(1) for Ḥassān ibn Thābit, and he would say to him: "Say, and the Holy Spirit is with you; satirize them, and Jibrīl is with you."(2) And he said to Kaʿb ibn Mālik(3): "Satirize them, for your speech is more painful to them than a volley of arrows."(4) He also permitted them to recite poetry in the mosque, because they entered into this exception: they are of those who believe, do righteous deeds, and remember Allah often; they are the ones who defend Islam, extol the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), protect him, and ward off the tongues of the disbelievers from him.

The meaning of ﴿and defend themselves after they have been wronged... 227﴾ (al-Shuʿarāʾ) is that they were not foolish, nor did they begin the disbelievers with satire; rather, they defended themselves and repelled the wrong that the disbelievers had inflicted upon Islam. Therefore, when Abū Sufyān satirized the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), one of them(5) replied to them:

"Do you satirize him, when you are not his equal?
So let the worse of you be a ransom for the better.
For my father, his father, and my honour
Are a shield against your attack upon the honour of Muḥammad."

As for the Exalted's saying ﴿after they have been wronged... 227﴾ (al-Shuʿarāʾ): wronged by whom? By those who took a hostile stance toward the religion and the Messenger, who confronted the Messenger of Allah and the believers in him with harm and plotting, who wronged the Messenger of Allah and his family by confining them in the valley (al-Shiʿb) until they ate the leaves of trees, and by those who conspired to kill him (ﷺ) until he migrated.

And from His mercy and wisdom, the Exalted permitted the wronged to defend himself and to vent through it what he suffers under the weight of injustice, so that these feelings are not suppressed within him and must erupt. He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And if you retaliate, then retaliate with the like of that with which you were afflicted; but if you are patient, it is better for the patient﴾ (al-Naḥl, 126).

And He said: ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech except by one who has been wronged...﴾ (al-Nisāʾ, 148).

Thus He permitted the wronged to express himself and to reject injustice, and there is no blame upon him if he speaks out with a word that eases what he feels of injustice.

Then the surah concludes with His saying: ﴿And those who have done wrong will come to know what a [dreadful] return they will be returned to﴾ (al-Shuʿarāʾ, 227), meaning: tomorrow they will know what their return and end will be, and what the destiny awaiting them is. "Al-munqalab" is the return and the place of return, and the outcome that awaits them.

So the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, threatens them with what will harm and grieve them. The matter will not end with the victory of the Muslims over them; rather, another recompense awaits them in the Hereafter.

As He, glory be to Him, said elsewhere: ﴿And indeed, for those who have done wrong is a punishment besides that...﴾ (al-Ṭūr, 47).

Therefore Allah, exalted is He, left this "munqalab" indeterminate, and its indeterminacy is for magnification and awe-inspiring effect. Its greatness has reached the point that it cannot be described, nor can expression convey its reality, just as He left the punishment indeterminate in His saying: ﴿Then there covered them of the sea that which covered them﴾ (Ṭā-Hā, 78).

That is: a great thing that cannot be told. The indeterminacy here is more eloquent, because the mind goes off in every direction in imagining it, and in every manner.

The "munqalab," or return, is not praised or blamed in itself: if it ends in evil, it is an evil return; if it ends in good, it is a good return. So what we are concerned with, the return of the disbelievers who oppose the Messenger of Allah, is an evil return that is blameworthy.

As for the return of Pharaoh's sorcerers, for example, when he said to them: ﴿Have you believed in him before I give you permission? Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides...﴾ (Ṭā-Hā, 71).

What did they say? ﴿They said: "No harm. Indeed, to our Lord we are returning"﴾ (al-Shuʿarāʾ, 50). This is a good return, praised and commended.

A person may think his return will be good, and that he will end up in what pleases him, while he is deluded and deceived in his deeds, expecting good; and Allah, exalted is He, mentions another return, like that of the man to whom Allah gave two gardens of grapevines, surrounded them with date palms, and placed fields between them. When the bounty of this world deceived him, he thought he would have the like of it, or better than it, in the Hereafter, and said: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a return﴾ (al-Kahf, 36).

The return and the resort to Allah, exalted is He, is only something to rejoice in for one who believes in Allah and does righteous deeds, because he knows that he will arrive at a recompense from the Truth, glory be to Him, that is certain. Therefore the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, teaches us, when we ride the animals that carry us: ﴿and they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship...﴾ (al-Naḥl, 7).

He taught us to mention Him: ﴿And the One who created all the pairs and made for you from the ships and the cattle that which you ride, so that you may sit upon their backs and then remember the favour of your Lord when you are seated upon them, and say: "Exalted is He who has subjected these to us, and we could not have subdued them. And indeed, to our Lord we will be returning"﴾ (al-Zukhruf, 12–14).

So the animals, and what now takes their place of means of transport, are among the greatest blessings of Allah upon us; and had Allah not subjected them to us, we would have had no power over them nor capacity to subdue them. Therefore we say: ﴿And we could not have subdued them﴾ (al-Zukhruf, 13).

That is: we cannot tame it. We see a small child leading a huge camel, making it kneel and loading it with burdens while it submits obediently; yet it panics if it sees a small snake. Why? Because Allah, exalted is He, subjected the camel to us and tamed it, and did not subject the snake to us.

And Allah the Mighty has spoken truly when He says: ﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, from what Our hands have made, livestock, and they are their owners? And We have subjected them to them, so some of them are for their riding and some of them they eat﴾ (Yā-Sīn, 71–72).

But what is the connection between our saying ﴿Exalted is He who has subjected these to us, and we could not have subdued them﴾ (al-Zukhruf, 13) and our saying ﴿And indeed, to our Lord we will be returning﴾ (al-Zukhruf, 14)?

They said: because we will return to Allah in the Hereafter, and we will be questioned about this blessing. If we thank our Lord for this blessing, we have fulfilled its right; and whoever thanks Allah for a blessing in this world will not be questioned about it in the Hereafter, because he has discharged its right.

And He said: ﴿And those who have done wrong will come to know...﴾ (al-Shuʿarāʾ, 227), with the sīn that denotes the future, but it does not mean a long time as some suppose; for Allah has concealed the time of death, and concealed its cause and place. This indeterminacy of death is itself the clearest explanation, because in this case you will await it and expect it at every moment, at every moment; and if a person knew the time of his death, he would say: "I will do what I want, then repent before I die."

So the time indicated by the sīn here is not long, for death may surprise you, and after death there is no work or repentance. Read His saying: ﴿As if, on the day they see it, they had not remained but an evening or its morning﴾ (al-Nāziʿāt, 46).

We have said that in the verse ﴿And those who have done wrong will come to know what a [dreadful] return they will be returned to﴾ (al-Shuʿarāʾ, 227) there is a warning and a threat. The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, when He magnifies the threat, intends only mercy toward His creation, and He loves them; so He threatens them now so that they may be saved tomorrow, and warns them so that they may return to Him and attain His recompense and mercy.

It is as if He, blessed and exalted, through this threat wishes to distribute His mercy rather than His might, just as you are harsh with your son so that he studies, and threaten him so that he strives. So the promise of good is good, and the warning of evil is also good; whatever comes to you from your Lord, know that it is good for you, even if it is a threat and a warning.

Thus the Surah of al-Shuʿarāʾ has presented us with a model of the consolation of the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, to His Prophet Muḥammad (ﷺ), and of easing for him what he meets of grief and pain over the condition of his people and their unbelief. It presented to him (ﷺ) the procession of the messengers, and how Allah supported and helped them, defeated their enemies and repulsed them.

Then his Lord consoled him by responding to the disbelievers in their fabrications, refuting their arguments, and showing the falsity of their claims. Then this consolation concludes with a clarification that the wrongdoers have an evil end awaiting them, and He left this end indeterminate, ﴿what [dreadful] return they will be returned to﴾ (al-Shuʿarāʾ, 227), in order to magnify it.

When a thing is specified, it comes in one form; but when it is left indeterminate, it is more eloquent, because the soul goes off in every direction in imagining it, just as when a traveller is late in returning at his appointed time, we sit waiting for him in anxiety, while doubts roam in us about the cause of his delay and the possibilities of what may have happened, and every illusion that enters the mind does so with pain and sting, whereas the reality is one thing.

(1) Surah al-Shuʿarāʾ is surah number 26 in the order of the Noble Qur'an; its verses number 227; it is a Meccan surah according to the majority view; in order of revelation it is surah number 46, revealed after surah al-Wāqiʿa and before surah al-Naml (see al-Itqān fi ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān by al-Suyūṭī, 1/27). Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda excepted four verses from it, which were revealed in Medina, from His saying {And the poets—the deviators follow them, 224} (al-Shuʿarāʾ) to the end of the surah. (Mentioned by al-Qurṭubī in his tafsīr, 7/4965).
